Who new Tuscon had a trendy downtown Mexican place? 
This restaurant has a nice clean, modern art atmoshere, with friendly people who look clean and polished in a southwestern way. 
Food is very good, with some pleasant and unusual refinements to standard Mexican faire, and usually they have several well thought out and tantalizing specials for the day chosen by the Chef/owner. There is patio seating as well as the dining room and bar. It is a very nice place to relax, even for the jaded California types.

If you are in Tuscon and craving sushi, this is a good choice. The place has a long sushi bar and several chefs. The head Sushi chef is Japanese, but most of the others are Korean. Pretty fresh seafood for the middle of the desert, and the prices are reasonable. You can get some Korean dishes here, too.

This is actually Sachiko Sushi II, the originall being off Speedway on Wilmot. Sachiko is the daughter's name of the Japanese owner and his Korean wife. There about 4 other eateries of different sorts next to this sushi-ya. 

It is pretty large, with 10 sushi bar seats and another 20 or so tables. When I went (Monday night) the chefs were both Korean, the young man from Seoul and the young woman from Fresno (second generation). The middle aged waitresses included a Korean and  Chinese-Vietnamese. This gave me a chance to practice saying thank you in Korean and Chinese, discuss Vietnamese food, ask for the best Korean restaurant in Tucson (there are none, according to the Koreans) and order and ask for the check in Japanese (which they understood), although they didn't try to welcome me with the Korean version of "Irashaiimase"!

I ordered my usual Nigiri choices, which came on the traditional wood platter. The sushi was all reasonably fresh and cut large, with smallish rice balls, but looked colorful. My chef (from Fresno) used very little wasabi on each piece, less than normal. Most common nigiri are priced at $3.50 (i.e. maguro, hamachi, sake, ebi, tako, saba, ika, izumi dai) and at $4.50 were unagi, anago, hirame, ikura. Cali roll is $4.50, Spicy Tuna roll is $4.50, Shrimp Tempura roll is $5.95 and Rainbow roll is $8.50 ( I didn't eat all of these, I am just telling you the prices!) Miso Shiro was free. 6 nigiri and a large Asahi beer totalled under $30 before tip. 

For a middle of the desert, Korean chefed sushi-ya, this place meets reasonable expectations for what it is and would satisfy most of the clients that come here (many of whom don't know better). There was even a table of Japanese businessmen eating, for lack of a more authentic alternative nearby.

Char's Thai has been voted the best Thai in Tucson for many years by Tucson Weekly and Tucson Traveler magazines. For Tucson, it is pretty good, but average at best if it was in a bigger pond. 

Their lunch specials are very reasonable: For $5.95 you get a choice of 9 mains that are served with fried rice, 2 fried WonTon, an Eggroll, and the soup of the day. I tried the Thai Curry, and although it is not offered on the menu, I asked and got Tofu instead of Beef, Chicken or Pork. The Thai ice coffee was $1.25. So this place is reasonably priced. But one thing that bugs me is the veggies...rippled carrot slices and baby corn. This is obviously not fresh, although the other veggies were.

This baby corn and ruffled carrot slices, where did it get started at Asian restaurants? I can trace it back to cheap Cantonese restaurants in SF Chinatown, but maybe before that? They probably couldn't get Gai Lan or Bok Choy way back then, so some one must have told them Americans like baby corn! Either that or the canned baby corn and carrots vendor had one hell of a salesman! Because it is used as cheap filler at so many cheap asian restaurants! Now let's think, is corn a popular and ubiquitous crop in Thailand? China? Korea? Rice, yes, Corn, no! So why is it used in these dishes at these places?  I digress...

Char's offers a wide variety of dishes, from your Mee Krob (sweet crispy noodles) and Yum Yai (Thai salad) appetizers, to Tom Yum soup, to 50 different entrees. You can order in mild, medium (the default), or Hot. 

It is in a strip mall near Rincon High School. It is affiliated with another Thai restaurant within the family, Bai Toung, which I think is over on Speedway.

Korea House has been around since 1984, so it has been either pretty good or perhaps had very little competition. I think it is the latter, as the tastes are so-so! Tucson can't compare to SoCal, the Bay Area, or the Pugent Sound for Korean food. This passes by with enough Korean influences to compensate for the sparse Korean restaurant choices in Tucson.

It is a prety large place, with private rooms on the left and on the right are the lowered Korean or Family type tables like in a Japanese Tatami room, except it is hardwood floors. 

KBBQ popular favorites like Bool Gogi (I am using their spelling) and Kalbi are available, for $13.95 and $18.00 respectively for beef. They only offer 5 side-dishes, less than most West Coast restaurants. They also have another 20 common rice, soup, and noodle dishes, like Bibeem Bob ($8.95 or $11.50in hot stone bowl), Naeng Myon (cold buckwheat noodles $9.25, ) and Tofu Soup ($9.95). They offer 6 vegetarians dishes, too.  

Their lunch specials are all between $6.25 - $9.75 and are served with Rice and Kimchee.

The Old Pueblo Grille has been around awhile, and used to be an old ranch. The gated grounds are large and feature a large patio, perfect for those warm spring or fall evenings in Tucson to dine outside. The adobe architecture creates a nice ambiance. It is part of the Metro Restaurant Group, which has about a dozen fine restaurants in the area.

The food is American with a decidedly Southwest influence. 
A large appetizer of Guacamole and Chips ($8.5), and Salsa ($5) is a good starter, but they have a lot of others more esoteric, like Rattlesnake Eggs ($9), or Coconut Shrimp ($9.5)

Our group of three tried the AZ Spiced Flat Iron Steak (Garlic butter, chipotle garlic mashed potatoes and seasonal vegetables $14.5); Cilantro Cream Stuffed Chicken Breast (chipotle garlic mashed potatoes, seasonal vegetables and sweet pasilla chile cream $14.5);
and the Chile Dusted Salmon (honey mustard glaze, chipotle garlic mashed potatoes and seasonal vegetables $15.5) 

All were very good and tasty, with a nice blend of southwestern flavors that didn't overpower the main entree. Grey Goose Vodka Tonic ($7) and Metro Margaritas ($6.95) followed us from the bar. 

Service was attentive if not a bit forward; the young waiter needed to relax a bit more rather than push us on his assertive timetable. (He was from Minnesota, you betcha!)

This is a great place for a good meal, at reasonable prices. There are some good menu choices to choose from. They offer lunch and dinner, and on Sundays have live Jazz.

Ever see old black and white TV shows about Daniel Boone, or Davy Crockett? See the guy in the racoon fur hat? That actor is Fess Parker, who has become a real estate developer, vineyard owner, and winemaker with his family in the Santa Barbara area over the past 30 years. Not bad for a former Disney actor. Read more about him:

http://www.fessparker.com/fess_parker.htm

The Cafe Los Arcos is inside the sprawling 23 acre Fess Parker's DoubleTree resort, right on the main beach at Santa Barbara on Cabrillo Boulevard. The resort is a beautiful venue, and ideal for meetings and conferences, with its 45,000 square feet of meeting space and lovely ocean views (well, minus the Oil Drilling Platforms that destroy the beautiful horizon. Thanks, former governor Reagan!)
It would be a great place for a wedding reception. 

The restaurant faces the ocean and has nice views of the beach and Volley Ball pits across the street. The service is excellent. The food is solid, with a bit of resort flair you would expect at a place that charges $240 - $350 per room (depending on day and season). 

If you come here just to eat, the parking lots are all gated and it will be about $3 for parking during your meal. However, if you show your receipt, it is free. 

According to the LA Times: Cafe Los Arcos has one major claim to fame: Channel Island fish chowder for $5.95 a bowl. Loaded with salmon, shrimp and scallops, this stuff is so thick a spoon could stand up in it. A bowl is a meal in itself.

Fess has a winery in the Santa Ynez valley in Los Osos, as well as another bed and breakfast inn nearby, all covering over 700 acres.

Not bad for a former Texan and TV star. 

The theme song to Davey Crockett was prophetic: "Davey, Davey Crockett, king of the wild frontier". (NOT sung to the tune of "Ventura Highway..in the sunshine, where the days are longer and the nights are stronger than moonshine..I wanna go, I know I know..")

The correct name for this is "Jack's Bistro and Famous Bagels."

 I guess when you are in Santa Barbara and own a Deli, you can call it a "Bistro", which nowadays means your restaurant is trying to be upscale, but it really serves sandwiches and coffee, with a few trendy salads, wraps, and panini bread  thrown in the the menu to tell you they are cool and you can be to if you only eat here.

Actually, this place has the espresso machines to serve beverages a la Starbucks, but they serve Peet's coffee. They have your standard American sandwiches, and "gourmet"?? sandwiches like Tuna Melt, Turkey Melt, Reuben, and a Vienna Hot Dog?? (that's gourmet?); and salads and soups, burgers, and pastas (well, only Fusilli and Penne, the "cool" pastas!). 

But really folks, this place is known for its breakfasts, served all day, like omelettes, burritos, of course Bagels, and things called Bagelwiches and B-Eggl'S (Like fast food Bagel Breakfast Sandwiches). 

There are 3 locations for Jacks. This one is in the "Trader Joe's Plaza" at the Milpas roundabout, where traffic congestion into and out of Highway 101 mixes with local street traffic into a European style roundabout, usually a haven for fender benders. 

Grab a bagel and watch the EMS vehicles arrive as you eat. Practice your rubbernecking skills sitting down in the outside patio.

Authentic Vietnamese food in Tucson? 

Believe it or not, yes! Ha Long Bay is Vietnamese owned, with Vietnamese staff. They offer all the main dishes you would find in a typical restaurant in San Jose, Westiminster, or  San Diego: Khai Vi, Canh, Pho, Mi, Hu Tieu, Com Tam, Bun, and even Boba Milk Tea and Smoothies. 

I had Pho Tai Bo Vien (rare beef and meatballs). The broth was pretty good, perhaps a little salty, probably a flavor preferred by the local customer base. $7.95, so expensive by $2 from a similar place in Little Saigon. Also had a Mango Bubble Smoothie, $3.50. 

The restaurant has been in business in about 5 years, and is neat and clean, with a nice decor of full wall murals of Ha Long Bay, with light fixture covers made of decorative traditional Vietnamese hats. 

It is open 7 days a week from 11 am until 9:30 pm. Grab a to-go menu and get a 10% discount coupon for your next meal.

This DoubleTree is an older property, a 9 story hotel near Reid Park.  However, they are in the midst of a remodeling campaign, and have updated the decor to a fresher, more modern appearance, with a mixture of soothing earth tones mixed with natural and bold geometric patterns. 

As at most DoubleTrees, they offer you a warm cookie when you check in to give you that "welcome home" feeling. However, checking in, the desk staff inadvertantly didn't return my credit card, but fortunately retrieved it after I left for awhile, put it in an envelope and left inside my room before I got there. 

It has pool, nail salon, and the Javelina Restaurant. This time of year (June) you can get a kingsize bed room with free internet for about $100. .

After getting them little doggies along, if you are hankering for a wrangled steak bigger than a ten gallon hat for less than a shot of whiskey and feed for your horse, then giddyup and high tail it down to the El Corral ranch  and hitch'er up. They would be much obliged.

Set at the foot of the Catalina mountains, this restaurant has been around since before the movie expression "Cut to the Chase" was the way to get to the climax of a silent western.

Set in an old ranch house that has added rooms as customers kept coming, this is an old school steak house that is down home and without any city slickers. 

"Petite" Prime Rib $11.95; In-bone Rib Eye $17.95, Porterhouse $17.95; all served with choice of soup or salad, and a side of baked or mashed potatoes, or Tamale Pie! We had 3 Golden Margaritas ($6.25) which is a margarita with a healthy splash of orange juice and  Grande Marnier; 3 Coronas ($4.25), 2 large Mudpies, 1 Strawberry Cheesecake (all $3.95) for a total less than $100 for the 3 of us before tax. 

Waitress was an old pro giving good service, and the food tasted great! 

If you can't get a square meal at home, then come on down to the El Corral and get your fill. You don't need to get all gussied up, either.

After this, you will kiss your horse and ride into the sunset with a smile.

This restaurant is on 2nd near Center in downtown Reno, across from Harrah's Casino on 2nd and half a block across Center and Cal-Neva Casino.

This was voted the #1  Vietnamese restaurant in 2007 by the Reno Gazette-Journal. (Well, there are only about half a dozen that exist in the Reno area that can challege it!)

I ordered Pho Tai Nam (rare and well done beef noodles) for lunch here. Small bowl is only $4.95, large a dollar more. I ordered the small bowl and a Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk, a standard, all totalling $7 and change. 

I must say that the broth is the most flavorful I have had in a long time, and I have eaten at 40 different Pho restaurants in the western US in just the past year! It was clear and flavorful like good Pho broth should be, suggesting that they use slow cook methods to develop a hearty stock without muddying it up. It was  missing that little extra hint of sweet fregrance that would have made it 5 stars on my list. The service was also a little slow.

What I do to perserve the good broth but get my condiment fix is to use the small condiment saucer found at most Pho places, and fill it half with Sriracha Tung Ot hot sauce and half Chinese oyster sauce, then dip the meat in this combo for a savory flavored mouthful before chasing it with a slurp of the noodles and tasty broth. I used to dump both sauces into the bowl, but that should be done when the broth is bleh! Whe it is good, try tis method. Always taste your broth first, too!

The place is very popular, and it has dozens of other dishes besides Pho. It has the typical Viet Pho set up: Older man comes and takes your order on a smalll pad, exept in my case he brought it out, too, then the latino busboys clean up . (Usually the latino would bring out the bowl in a lot of places!) 

No 42 inch plasma TV showing Vietnamese variety shows on DVD, though, which is almost ubiquitous in Little Saigon in SoCal and becoming almost as common in San Jose and other Vietnamese and Korean joints. They also don't have the little gold and black numbers on each table, which most Pho places have, they just remember the table numbers like most Denny's would do. The decor is plain and frugal and the place is reasonable size, seating maybe 50 -60 people in a turn. It is not spotless, but acceptable for a inexpensive Pho place, and not as dingy as some I have been in.

Turns out it is right across the street from Harrah's "Lucky Noodle" restaurant, and should be tried instead if you are staying or gambling at Harrah's or other nearby hotels and you want your Pho fix!

It is open 7 days a week, 10am till 9pm.

.

Well, Fin Fish must have heard the 1 star disappointments of the previous 2 reviews 4 months ago, and stepped up their game big time!

I came on a weekday evening, and sat at the many counter dining seats. Joe was my service person, and he was quite knowledgable and attentive. They have a variety of seafood, but I opted for the 3 course fixed price menu with wine pairings, entitled "Nova Scotia Coastal Passport".

1st Course: Wild Atlantic Smoked Salmon slices on a crisp potato cake with Horseradish Creme Fraiche.  A duet of these were served, nicely plated and presented with minced basil leaves and sprinkled with olive oil, and included red raddish slices. It was paired with a 
Maso Canali Pinot Grigio, which had nice apple/pear flavors and a clean finish. This was a nicely suited combo, although I would have prefered a slightly crisper potato to contrast the textures and reduce the oiliness. 

Course #2:  Bacon wrapped Cod, Chanterelle mushrooms, served on a bed of Sweet Corn. This was nicely paired with a Syrah, from the Okanagen area of BC Canada. The Syrah, being from a cooler climate, limited its tanin and body, making it a nice compliment to the Cod, and the crisp bacon wrap added texture and more flavor, which was well balanced by the mushrooms and especially the sweet corn.

Course #3: Spiced Ginger Bread, Carmelized Maple Syrup and Blueberry preserves. This dessert course was paired with a nice Jackson Triggs Niagara Peninsula Vidal Ice-Wine.  I am not big on desserts, but this was a nice combo. The ginger bread would have been good without the overly sweet icing on its layers, because the sweetness of the Ice Wine, so called due to the very late harvest (ergo Ice, when the water content is low but the flavors and sugars are stronger) was sweet enough for my palette. 

All pairings were well executed and elegantly plated without too much pompous stacking. You would expect to pay perhaps $100 in SF or LA for this 3 course meal and wine pairing. 

The cost? Only $44 per person, and only $33 without the pairings. Excellent value!

This Starbucks is a concession inside the Grand Sierra Resort, formerly the Hilton, and before that, formerly the MGM Grand Reno. It is located near the main casino floor near the other shops and not too far from one of the main bars, and also not far from Registration.   

Ready made Sandwich $5.50
Grande Soy Latte $4.15

This is inside the Grand Sierra resort, which is on Second Street, ergo the place is cleverly called the 2nd Street Express.  It is a casual sandwich shop. It uses the "express" part of its name loosely, as it is a bit inefficient.

The girl at the counter takes your order, rings you up and takes your money. She may give you a self-serve drink cup, too. She gives the food order to the cook. No number system, no name system.

The hot stuff is made by the cook, who is behind a very high counter. 
When she has made your order, she softly says the name of what she has made, and sort of waits for a response from anyone within 2 feet of her, while the other orders cook away unattended. IF you didn't hear her becuase most of the tables are around the corner  of the space, your food gets cold. 

Suggestion: grab and go a sandwich and fruit cup with a soda cup. 

Turkey Pesto Sandwich $7.50. Fruit salad $4.00. Soda $2.50. It is all self serve, so not particularly a bargain.

I don't know what is so great about Hollister, California. 

I used to go out to Hollister to visit cousins twice removed, and it was boring out there. Maybe now with the growth of Silicon Valley 40 miles to the north, Hollister has improved? I doubt it. 

So why would you create an entire clothing line called Hollister? Does that sound better than Banana Republic or Abercrombie and Fitch?

IF there is no good reason for a clothing line named Hollister, why a brew pub restaurant?

This restaurant is in a shopping mall between the 101 freeway and the UC Santa Barbara campus. 

It is another one of the now popular mini-brewery restaurant and sports bar. It is clean, large, nice, and friendly. Food is typical for this type of establishment. They do have a decent selection of beers, and the staff is knowledgeable in them. 

I couldn't make up my mind, so I went for the 6 pack sampler, for only  $7. I told the bartender to surprise me. They were good. They help wash down the Pulled Pork Sandwich ($12), which was on the dry side. 

Mondays is Pint Night, with select house beers for only $3. 
Tuesday is Brewer's Choice. $2.50 pints and $10 pitchers, ALL DAY!
Saturday is Growler Night. $13 new, $6.50 refills. 

By the way, Hollister is one of the most earthquake prone cities in California. But if you drink enough beer here at Hollister Brewing in Goleta, you'll never feel the shaking up there in the real Hollister.

Kyoto Restuarant in Santa Barbara has been around since 1981, but over the years, its has been open with 5 different owners. Currently it is Korean owned and Sushi Chefs are Korean, too, although like most Korean owned Japanese Restaurants, they have learned how to say "Welcome" in Japanese to fool the non-Japanese who come here. 
(Hai, Irashai, [Yes, Welcome] Irashaimasen [Welcome, a little more formally])

Aside from the little Sushi Bar, Kyoto has a pretty complete menu of traditional Japanese dishes, Hibachi grill items like Yakitori or Saba Shioyaki and about 4 different Teriyaki; Tempura, Noodles like Udon and Soba, including cold Zaru Soba and fried Yaki Soba, and Sukiyaki. They even have Oju dishes, which you might recognize as Donburi (Tempura, pork cutlet or chicken/egg over a large rice bowl.) Although Una Ju (Eel) is usually served in a special little bento like dish with a cover.

They do have 3 larger combo Special meals, too. They have a very reasonable mix and match Lunch special for only $7.95, so prices are reasonable here, and they have a lot of local regulars, although business is slow right now. 

And of course, being Korean owned, they offer a Yaku Niku, which is a Japanese version of Korean Barbeque. 

Imagine that: A Korean owned Japanese restaurant offering a Japanese version of the classic Korean barbeque, eaten by Caucasians in Santa Barbara, home to the Haas Avacado, which is popular in a California Roll, which is a US invention and is hard to find in Japan.

I am confused!

Think about it: 

- you are in Boise, Idaho, a place called the "City of Trees" only because everywhere outside this valley are foothills covered with prairie tumbleweed and prairie dog poo, with nary a tree in sight.
- you are farther east and farther inland than Las Vegas, Nevada
- you are in a place better known for potatoes than rice
- the Asian population is miniscule

So why are you looking for Sushi here? 

Turns out, Fujiyama, which means Mount Fuji and is named after the famous, perfectly coned shaped tallest mountain in Japan so ingrained in its heritage, art and lore, is the name of this restaurant. They have bright pictures of Fujiyama behind the sushi bar, and truth be told, the sushi is not bad, all the above considered! 

Although it is definitely decorated in a motif decidely Japanese restaurant, the place is Chinese owned (for the past 9 years), operated and staffed. The owners are a youngish couple from Fujian, China, and speak Mandarin to their little toddler child. The sushi chefs are pretty decent, and are also Chinese. And the waitresses are also CHinese, but speak English. So save your Japanese or Korean, and practice your hsieh hsieh in poh tung wua.  

Unlike so many Korean and Chinese owned sushi-ya in other cities (i.e. most of California) that scrimp on the rice balls, and cut the sushi too thin so it appears like you are getting more than you deserve, these guys conform their sushi rice balls pretty close to what you find in Japan,and their slices of fish are close, too. They don't put a dab of wasabi under the fish like you would find on 95% of sushi in Japan, but most places here don't do this, and rather in the American tradition, let you put the wasabi in your soy sauce dish to taste. (In Japan, usually the wasabi is in the sushi, and you dip it only in soy sauce.) But most people would be confused by this here. 

They have a large menu, and they offer a lot more than sushi, with a good selection of other hot dishes from the kitchen, and the typical appetizers and casual dishes.

The service is quick and polite, and the presentation is good. I had my standard Nigiri selections and my associate had sashimi and was satisfied. We had edamame, 2 bowls of miso soup, and a double scoop of green tea ice cream dessert, gren tea, a diet coke, all for under $60 for two. 

This is perhaps the best sushi place in Boise, Idaho. It's average for the sushi haven cities on the west coast, but above average for Boise and above average for a Chinese owned sushi restaurant. I would come back.

So why are you looking for Sushi in Boise? 

Wo bo ju dou! 
(Wakaranai)
(I don't know)

Saigon 88 is run by the Huynh family from Saigon, VIetnam and it is a nice little treat of a place in Sparks in the CVS shopping mall across from the Iron Horse Mall at the corner of Prater and McCarran.

It has a nice clean decor, with green walls decorated with Vietnamese scenes in pleasing water colors and black frames, marble table tops, cherry wood seating,  track mini spot lights, and has smooth jazz playing on the speakers to add to the relaxed vibe atmosphere.

They have a limited menu, and combine both Vietnamese favorites like Cha Gio, Goi Cuon and Pho,  with Thai favorites like Tom Yum and Pad Thai. There is a selection of rice plates, too, and they have Hu Tieu, although they call it their seafood special. 

We had Cha Gio (egg rolls, 4 pieces), and Pho Tai and Pho Tai Nam (beef soup with rice noodles; rare round, and rare round and flank). They were served in classy Japanese styled ceramic decorative udon bowls, rather than those cheap plastic red and white Chinese bowls. They were only $6.50 for good sized bowls.  I was pleasantly surprised by the deep flavor of the beef broth, and it was fairly clear in color, not doctored up like some places. 

Since this was the 94th different Pho Noodle restaurant I have eaten in over the past 4 years, I have a little bit of knowledge of Pho, at least what I think is a good bowl. This was good, and the condiments were fresh and tasty as well.   The service was prompt and friendly. 

The Huynh family didn't get out of Vietnam until 1985, 10 years after the fall of Saigon to the Communists, so you can imagine the memories they have. But they came to California, did nails in San Francisco, and worked their way into this nice restaurant. So come here and support their business, because the food is pretty good and it is a pleasant dining experience at a reasonable price.

Well, if you've been to one In-n-Out, you've probably been to them all. 

This one is on Pyramid way, just of I-80 and a block from John Ascuaga's Nugget Casino and Resort. 

They have a formula that is pretty consistent. The same design inside, the same colors, the same white outfits, the same well scrubbed teens serving you and cutting fresh french fries, the same 3 combo meals. 

This one has a drive through, and at least during daylight hours, instead of the ordering squawk box, there is a young lady there to personally take you order and send it in. 

Then from there, you pay at the first window, and then pick up your order by the time you get to the second window. 

The entire crew is well trained and polite. 

The food is In-n-Out good.

The best thing about Hana Garden is that it is very reasonably priced! 

The lunch specials, which include rice and banchan, are all under $7 except for Kalbi which is $7.95. These are served between 11 - 3.

However, 4 of us came for dinner, and the prices are almost as low! 

We had 2 Dolsot Bibimbop, (sizzling claypot with rice, veggies and some beef) which was good sized and hot, with the egg already fried on top (many places put it in raw and let the heat cook it up), and 2 Kalbi boneless rib meat, a bottle of Jinro Soju, two sodas, and the bill was $66 after tax. 

The banchan were sparse (only 3 types, sprouts, tofu and kimchi), and the food wasn't as good as K-Town in LA.  But let's get real, this is Sparks, Nevada, where there are more  Christian and Latin radio stations on AM than there are total Asian restaurants of all types. 

They have a little Asian variety, perhaps to appeal to a broader client base, with appetizer dishes like Crab Rangoon ($3.95), Edamame ($2.95), Egg Roll ($3.95), Fried Dumplings ($3.95) and Calamari Tempura ($4.95). 

But they have traditional Korean favorites like Bulgogi ($8), Kalbi ($9), Dakguyi ($8), Jjamppong ($8), Jajamyun ($8), Naengmyun ($8), and Soon Dubu ($8) and Doenjang Soup ($8). They also have Udon, Ramen, Chicken Teriyaki and Chicken Katsu.   

The decor is simple and dinerish, and the service was friendly and efficient. 

I can see why local families and UNR foreign students come here for a tasty,  reasonably priced meal.

They are closed on Sundays, open the rest from 11am till 9pm.

Ijji Sushi is sort of like AYCE Sushi meets a Korean owned Chili's, or something like that. 

It appears to be Korean owned, with Latino Sushi Chefs and wait staff, serving Americanized Japanese food to all comers here in Sparks, Nevada. 

This place is huge, with dozens of tables and a long, long sushi bar that seats perhaps 30 people.  The decor is modern and new looking, pleasing and clean. The service is very attentive and on the spot, and friendly. 

The food is another matter. 

Like when you were a fussy eating kid at your parent's dinner table, this is one of those AYCE places that penalizes you for not eating all your food. NO, they don't make you do the dishes, and no starving kids in China and India will die because you didn't finish your plate. However, you will have to pay for your eyes being bigger than your stomach, it says so right on the menu. 

Personally, I don't like sushi places that are AYCE at all because the sushi is never good nor authentic.  And fearing a penalty is even more ridiculous and a good reason not to come.

So why did I come here? Well, there aren't that many Japanese restaurants in Sparks, Nevada, and this was the closest one I could find. I knew that hoping for good Asian food at Trader Dick's inside of John Ascuaga's Nugget wasn't going to serve me, well, a nugget of an authentic Asian meal. 

So we ordered combo Bento boxes for dinner. These sounded good and reasonable on the menu. But when I was served the Sashimi, Tempura and Salmon teriyaki combo, I was disappointed. The Sashimi consisted of 2 small slices of Salmon. That's it.  I was given a lot of edamame and salad to fill me up. The Tempura was meh at best with the wrong type of dipping bowl, and the Salmon was probably the best part at just OK.  At least the Salmon pieces were in the shape of fish. 

If you are from Sparks, Verdi, Mogul or Minden Nevada and eat Japanese food once every other year, this place may be great for you. Oyster shooters for you yahoos with your AYCE. But If you are from SF or LA, you may consider passing, or accept that it is what it is, if you are just desperate for some Asian flavors, not Japanese food. 

BTW, my favorite relative, who had chicken and beef teriyaki with california roll combo, had diarrhea for the next 48 hours after eating here. And she didn't have a shooter, at least not from her ingesting orifice.

Bangkok Cuisine Thai Restaurant has two locations, this one on Mt Rose in Reno, and another called Bangkok Cuisine South. There is also a Bangkok Cuisine Express, but not sure if it's the same ownership.

The restaurant looks small from the outside, with its warnings of what lot to park at as you walk in (pick the more obvious one next door and you may get towed, so park in the lot in the rear, not on the side!), but inside it is a bit larger, with a cozy atmosphere and quaint village-like decor and the obligatory picture of the Thai King and Queen near the kitchen. 

They are offering a 15% discount for Yelpers, so check in here and reveal the coupon on your iPhone and show your waitress, and they will take 15% off your bill (excluding alcohol)!.

The food is pretty good, and they offer a large and typical selection of Thai favorites at reasonable prices. They have perhaps a dozen Apps, ranging from $4 - $7, and if you can't make up your mind, you can get the sampler tray for $14: 2 Curry Pops, 1 Spring Roll, 2 Thai Sticks (not the weed, the Satay!), 2 Shrimp Tempura, 2 Shrimp Rangoons and mixed veggie Tempura. 

They have 10 salads including Papaya, Seafood Combo, Nam Sod, Duck Laub (in the $7 - $11 range). There are 8 different soups, a handful of noodle dishes (Pad Thai $9 or $10), Fried Rice dishes (4 to choose), and over 25 entrees, Curries, and House Specials (all $9 - $15 depending on meat selection).

They also have traditional desserts of deep fried bananas or sweet rice and mango ($5 or $6). 

The food was very tasty, perhaps a bit too salty but with good flavors, and the service was good. We had a little personal drama due to a mix-up of coke vs diet coke for a diabetic in our foursome, but other than that, it was a good place for Thai. 

Check out their website, it is informative and professional, with peaceful music.

John Ascuaga's Nugget used to be the pride of Sparks, Nevada. Sadly, there isn't a lot anything in Sparks to be of pride about, as the growth of Indian gaming in California, the emphasis on Las Vegas for Mega-Casinos, and the housing bust and economy have all taken their toll. 

I had never stayed at the Nugget in all my years, preferring around Lake Tahoe for skiing and gambling. I have been to Harrah's in downtown Reno, and the Grand Sierra before, and I had always heard from relatives who liked to go to Reno that the Nugget had a great Friday Seafood Buffet. 

The Nugget has twin towers of 29 floors each, connected in between with about a 5 story structure housing the restaurants, casino, convention center, and swimming pool. In fact, the swimming pool which is in an indoor atrium with 4 retractable picture windows, is probably the best thing about the Nugget. It is large, not very crowded, has 8 individual sized whirlpools, and a large donut shaped whirlpool with a donut hole island in the middle. There are plenty of chaise chairs, but not much sunlight, You have to go outside on the patio for that. There is also no food concessions that are open by the pool. So don't think "Resort" but more fancy YMCA. 

The hotel is situated by the railroad stock yards. The good thing is the Amtrak rail comes nearby, and the bus station is next door. But the bad thing is you hear diesel locomotive engines groaning on the rails at 3 in the morning. You better gamble and drink a lot of free stiff ones so you don't have to hear the mysterious sounds in the wee hours like a scary movie, or you'll have nightmares. 

The restaurants are meh. The buffet is below $30, but I didn't go there, just my friends told me about it. It is closed in the morning. The Deli in the Sports book in the basement is understaffed and service is slow, with a cafeteria like approach that would make similar airport establishments look like finely tuned models of efficiency. Rose's Cafe, the main diner type place, is your best choice, as the food is ok, reasonably priced, and the service is friendly. I didn't try Trader Dick's, but from what my friends told me, it is a poor man's Trader Vic's without near the same quality. THey also have a noodle bar somewhere on the property, and a finer dining place. 

The rooms are typical, kings our double queens, but few if any have microwaves, wet bars, flat screen (still CRT) or other amenities that newer hotels might have. Wifi is not free either, the best deal being a weekly rated for nearly $60. 

The Casino was small compared to Vegas standards, with only 2 craps tables, one roulette, a couple of dozen tables, and less slots than many California Indian Casinos. The good thing for you cheap low roller dice enthusiasts, is they have $2 craps here 24/7. The bad thing is, that table is as cold as ice! Trust me, I went to the well many times and came up with ice cubes, not hot dice. 

The group rate I got was $87 a night. 

I was attending a trade event here, so I didn't have a lot of choice in my accommodations. It was an event for the blind and visually impaired, and to that, they accommodated well the unsighted who came with canes and guide dogs galore with talking elevators and helpful service. One Craps croupier left his station and personally walked a blind person across from the East tower casino end to the West end. And John Ascuaga himself , all 5 ft nothing of him, came down and shook the hands of everyone working this event.  

That's class with a personal touch! But sadly, the hotel can't compete with all the things working against it today.

This is a great old school type steakhouse, with great steaks and excellent service. It's in the basement on Harrah's Reno.

By old school, I mean the waiters all wear tuxedos. And also hard to find these days, is traditional and original Caesar Salad made at the table by your server, with anchovies. They have a great recipe with a twist:

1 1/2 heads of romaine lettuce.
1/2 lemon
3 large strips anchovies
2 large cloves of chopped garlic
1 serving spoon worcestershire sauce
2 dashes of tabasco
1 tbs of Dijon mustard
2 serving spoons red wine vinegar
2 coddled egg yolks
3/4 cup of olive oil
1 1/2 cups croutons
1 cup parmeson cheese

I love a great Caesar salad like this made table side. The Dijon, which is a bit unusual, somehow blended well and took the salty edge off the Anchovies, and everyone liked it. (Recipe is for 4)

Our server was the Matre d'Captain of the steak house, Bong Genio. This little Filipino knew his stuff, was very professional, yet very entertaining and quick witted, with great timing and execution. 

Heavenly desserts, too, see my pics!

Our party of six had a variety of steaks, all tasty and cooked to our liking. We had a good old school meal here, and this place has been perhaps Reno's best restaurant since 1967.

I stopped here for a lunch quite awhile back. In fact, so long ago, I barely remember it, but then I did take a picture and the new Yelp software reminded me to review it. 

This is right off the 101 freeway, so it can be a passing through type of place, as well as a local place. There didn't seem to be a lot of locals, however, as it wasn't crowded, but I came a little bit at an odd time. 

It isn't a large place, and it has a bit of an old feel to it. I remember it being a bit dark, with furnishings, but not lively at all in feel or energy. The food is decent but not memorably outstanding, at least what I had. 

They are known for their menudo, but then, I wasn't drunk when I came, and we all know menudo is good hangover food. 

Service was ok, again, nothing memorable, or I would have written this review sooner!

This is located in the Skyway between the East and West Towers of the Harrah's in Reno. The same branded restaurant is in other Ceasar's Entertainment Group's other Harrah's properties in Vegas, New Orleans, etc. 

They serve sort of kitschy diner food with a twist. The menu selection is less, the portions are huge, (compared to your average diner) and everything seems to cost $13.95, from a Cobb salad, burger and fries, to other sandwiches. 

The best value, in my opinion, is The Basic breakfast, which is 2 eggs, potatoes, choice of ham, bacon or sausage, and buttered toast, for $8.99. The portions are large, served on a platter. It is served all day and night 

The aluminum decor themes in the chairs and accents meld with the earth tone Casino decor, with some retro posters to make a hodge podge ambiance suitable for anyone, at least partly. The cold aluminum chairs are not that inviting when you combine them with the Full Blast A/C that Harrah's likes to pump out...bordering on meat locker for you thin blooded types. 

I had a Salmon Burger with Sweet Potato fries. This huge, oversized breaded meat monster on top of a bun came out, not what I was expecting, criss-crossed in sauce strings like a bad yada yada whateva roll at your local Korean owned sushi place, (or Safeway). 

What they lack in taste and quality, they make up for in ginormous sizes.  Services was friendly and good, but it is a long walk for them back to the kitchen. Food came out pretty quick, too, but there was only a few tables taken, as I was here mid-week.  

They are open until midnight, so when everything else is closed around DTReno, you can go here.

UqveHrPl5-WZBUQiRcim-Q.review_text: Best Thai food I have had yet. The service was excellent.  Very nice. Will be visiting more frequently.
Very good food. Great mixture of food and the employees are very friendly. Nice little spot for a quick bite to eat.
Couldnt wait to go back. 2nd experience was just as good. Great food. Awesome service.  Might be my new favorite place.
Love the food and the service. I have ate breakfast there a few times and a few lunches and it has always been delicious. Great bartenders and food. What else can you ask for.
Love this place. Crispy wings, great pizza and best staff around. You should give them a try and I'm sure you wont be disappointed. Get a bucket of wings to go and I'm sure your party will be a hit.

Fist time going. Heard all the hype. Sat for 1 1/2 hours. My girlfriend and I ordered our food then got 2 completely different meals. Then the mgr came and told us there were 3 screw ups. The employees were all very nice. The food was good. Mix up ruined our time there. We sat outside and that was nice. We don't plan on going back anytime soon. We should of went to Thai Lotus. We didn't even try desserts. They did make it right with the bill. And my beer was 8.50
Closest bar to my house. Always good food and great staff. Bar is always full of regulars and they have 2 happy hours. Cant go wrong.

My second time eating at Jimmy Johns, first time was great. Was at a different location. Last night 11/12/14 went to the new one off Longley and wasn't impressed. My bread was hard and was cracking while i ate it. They coated my girlfriends lettuce wrap with mayonnaise. Should have went somewhere else.

After seeing a sub my coworker brought back from lunch i took a pic and sent it to my girlfriend. Next day we went. We love yellow sub now. Bring your appetite as they are stuffed with deliciousness. Small inside and the dolls are a little creepy but food is so good. I recommend them to everyone now.

We come here often. They show support to my children's school and have a school or family donation day once a month which i think is great. There food has always been good. Fast service and friendly.  I probably should of given them a 5.
Pizza was great.. Kids were running around and no one complained. Had a good time there. Now off to bowling

Our first experience was from a living social deal. Never a real risk when its a deal. We stood at the door for 5 minutes before being seated. Once sat waited probably 10 minutes before my girlfriend got up to track down menus. Already upset we finally got to order. The food was great. The desert was great. We got to talk with the owner for a bit who was very friendly. If we left before talking to him we would of never gone back. The last 2 times we went we got much better service. I choose 3 stars to be fair. The food is great. Worth trying for yourself.

We love the food here which is why we come back even with the horrible service. Last 5 times we have been in its dead but still takes a while to get your order. Outstanding! Love that they make the sushi in front of u. Enjoy the veg options. I'm gf and the the guy was knowlgable about what sauces were safe for me. I love wasabi and anywhere I go I get a tiny tiny pinch of wasabi. So happy at the condiment station I can grab as much as i need
