We stopped in here for a late lunch/early dinner, having read a terrific review in The Scene. As other reviews noted, their "hot" is truly "hot", and like the hot at Smiling Elephant, it still has flavor. That's the plus side.
We over-ordered, meaning to take leftovers home. The shrimp dumplings were good - about the same as Smiling Elephant. One of us had the drunken noodles with added shrimp - a total of $16.95, which I thought was pretty steep for 6 small to medium shrimp, a lot of noodles, and some vegetables. Still, the dish was terrific. He ordered it "hot" and even though I'm not a huge fan of over-spicing, it was delicious.
That's the good news.
Now, on to the bad. 
"Do you have sparkling water?" No. "What about club soda?" No. "Ginger ale?" No. The "full bar" means bottled beer, a few bottles of decent liquor, but no ability to mix with anything from a soda nozzle.
For me, one of the hallmarks of any Asian restaurant is the rice. I was pleased when our waitress asked whether I wanted sticky or not, and asked for sticky. When it came, it was so old and over-cooked that it stuck together to the point where I lifted about half a cup out on my spoon and held it over the table, upside down. Overcooked, dry, bad enough that I sent it back. The rice that came to replace it was (I think) just the same rice, with newer rice on the top. Also overcooked, and crunchy with age.
I ordered the deep-fried spareribs (I have been dreaming of Chinese spareribs lately, and unable to find good ones when I visit Nashville). I expected they'd have a hard crust outside, and be tender inside, but not so. Through and through they were so tough it was difficult to eat more than a few bites. And the salt! Unbelievable. Even I, who carries salt in my suitcase and on my person "just in case", found them inedible.
Two major tests of Thai food for me are Larb Gai, and Tom Yum soup. The soup was inedible - twice the vinegar it should have had, and loads of sugar to cut it. Actually, it may have been the worst Tom Yum I've ever had.
The Larb Gai (chicken larb) was very disappointing. Greasy and over-oiled, to the point where I had to pour oil out of the plate because as it got cold, it began to congeal.
Which brings me to another point. The Larb tasted like it had been pre-made, then microwaved to heat it up. The telltale sign was that it was nice and hot when served, but cooled almost immediately.
We had plenty of leftovers. We didn't take anything home. That about sums it up. I'm willing to go back because the Drunken Noodle dish was so good, but as I said to my colleagues - when four out of five dishes are bad, it may not be worth a return trip.
Also, I think it's extremely expensive for what you get. Extremely. I don't mind spending a fair amount of money if I get a fair amount of value, but I DO mind spending what amounted to $20 per person (with no liquor) for a below-average, greasy meal.
It's unfortunate, because the building itself is beautiful.

When Bob Bernstein first announced he was opening a Northeastern-style "diner", my family was pretty excited. Visiting one at Vanderbilt, we made plans well ahead of time for breakfast with the family. 
Breakfast was ok. Grits were good. It was pricey. Staff were friendly. It was noisy. We all agreed that for half the money, we could have had essentially the same thing at Wholly Chow or even Athens, but since it was a Bob Bernstein (of Bongo Java and Fido fame) restaurant, we assumed the quality of goods would be better. Eh. And loads of sugar. 

Still, we were curious to try the lunch/dinner menu - though to be honest, after looking at it we were not nearly so curious. Diner food? Really? 
The word "fussy" has been used to describe the menu. I'd agree, along with "Created-by-someone-very-young-who-never-visited-a-real-diner-before". Or ate a Philly cheese steak, a decent patty melt, or homemade aioli.
We entered at about 2 pm on a weekday, to be greeted by a pink-haired waitress who seemed surprised that we wanted to sit at a table rather than the counter. We assumed she'd seat us at one of the dozen or more empty tables, already set with dishes and silver, but it was not to be. She found the one table that needed busing, took her time clearing it, and finally returned to seat us. By then we were already irritated by the high volume of music, not to mention being seated at the back of the room when there were plenty of light tables available. But my wife doesn't like to "make a scene", so there we were.
The waitress was lovely. No, they don't have any soda water. No, they don't have seltzer either. They do have water, which was served in a nice bottle.
I questioned the roast beef sandwich, described only as "roast beef, caramelized onions, gruyere, horseradish aioli, French roll, au jus." Yes, it was delicious. No, the roll wasn't really a baguette. Or French. Or crusty. Yes, I could have the aioli on the side. Being the diner-friendly person I am, I assumed this would either be shaved roast beef off a nice roast (the menu doesn't specify antibiotic-free or locally obtained, but I hoped), or a nice healthy piece of roast beef, the sort you'd get at J. Alexander's when you order a French Dip. In fact, the waitress even described it as a French Dip.
My two friends ordered the patty melt, "two gourmet pasture beef patties" etc etc, with "dijonnaise sourdough."
How do I describe how indescribably bad this meal was? We all three agreed that our sandwiches were the worst we'd ever had. That's saying a lot, for three people who travel constantly and are often stuck eating hotel food or Denny's.
My friends each had a few bites of their patty melts, then ate their salads instead. Which looked fresh enough, although it would have been nice if someone had made an attempt to dry the lettuce before plopping it onto the plates. 
The aioli was tasteless. How that's possible is beyond me. I asked for horseradish on the side. They had no horseradish. "How is the horseradish aioli made, then?" No answer. My friends asked for mayonnaise. They had no mayonnaise. "How is the aioli made, then?" No answer. 
The "au jus" was anything but; straight from a can, or possibly a carton, and doctored with an unidentifiable spice that made it hot to the tongue and unpleasant to the nose.
The creamy parmesan salad dressing was all right, once I'd added salt and a lot of pepper. At least, it was better than the pseudo-aioli.
The "French bread" was what you'd expect from a Southern supermarket - soft, white, and thanks to the chef, greasy. 
But the real astonishment was inside the sandwich. Shaved pieces of beef that looked - and tasted - like they'd been sitting in a fridge all day (I hope), burned around the edges, and again, completely tasteless. The "Gruyere" cheese was unlike any Gruyere I've ever known; no bite to it, no taste to it. The "caramelized onions" were cooked through, and browned, and damp. And tasteless.
The sandwich looked like someone's idea of a Philly cheese steak, without the good beef, without the good cheese, without the fresh-cooked onions, and without the good bread. 
I tried it with the aioli; no improvement. I tried it with the parmesan dressing; slight improvement. I gave up after that. Between the strange condiments in the lukewarm "au jus", the greasy bread, the over-done meat and wretched onions, I couldn't finish any more.
How to describe the meal? Here's how bad it was. We couldn't get the taste of the food out of our mouths. Rather than spend a ridiculous amount of money on coffee there, we drove down to the nearest gas station and purchased 3 small coffees, drowning our sorrows in them.
Normally, I would give a new restaurant three tries, but after such an awful experience, I'm not willing to risk it. 
This is not a diner. It's an experiment in bad taste, literally. A real pity.

Good: 
A beautiful space, located in an up-and-coming area you wouldn't have wanted to visit 3 years ago. You walk in and immediately feel at home. The whole club, from bar area to bathrooms to the showroom, is intimate without being cloying. 
It fills a huge gap in this city, which has needed an upscale club inbetween tiny 75-100 seaters (eg Bluebird Café) and larger halls (Ryman). 
Very clean, great bathrooms, nice bar area. Lots and lots of wood.
They're making their own wine next year, and the gigantic barrels are eye candy if you like good vino. The wine lists (there are 2) are comprehensive. Some very reasonably priced , but that's because they charge YOU the liquor tax. Be forewarned.
Food is better than expected. Risotto balls, recommended by our waitress, were excellent (though I'd go for spicier mustard). Pork tacos ditto. The steak was two lovely pieces of meat - though the chef has a heavy salt hand. (Maybe they're salting and letting it sit to tenderize? Still, it shouldn't be that salty.) I don't recommend the mussels, and the cheese tray is absurdly small for what you pay, but the ravioli was gorgeous. The burgers are very good, and there's a vegetarian option too.
I'd recommend the meze platter, except that we had it our first visit (opening night) and it was large enough for four. Last visit it had shrunk considerably. 

The bad: 
Five dollar parking charge? Really? The attendants make it clear that your $5 goes to the venue, so you're expected to tip on top of it. But there's NO street parking!!
Getting seated is a work in progress. I've been here 5 times so far, alone, with family, with business associates. Each time, we arrived at 6 pm, when they opened. Each time, wait staff weren't ready. Each time, there's a meaningless cluster of hosts and hostesses? standing by the entry doors, doing anything but paying attention to the customers. Each time we were sent to the "concierge" for tickets and information. Forgive my being snotty about it, but how many City Winery employees does it take to seat someone? If it happened once, all right. But every time? 
Food service is slooooow. Don't come hungry. I don't know if the wait staff are over-loaded or what, but when you go out for an expensive evening like this, you expect better service. My waitrons have all been nice, but far from the kind of competency I experienced at the NY or Chicago clubs.
Food is expensive for what you get. (Online menu prices changed?) Our party of four had a bottle of inexpensive wine, 3 Tito's vodkas, and two beers, plus mains and 2 appetizers) was $310 before tip. I think that's expensive. Portions aren't big enough for leftovers. If this were The Palm, I'd expect it, and I'd be satisfied knowing the quality would be wonderful AND I'd have enough for another meal next day. 
The wait staff are friendly, but scattered. Ask for salt and pepper. Ask again. And again. Finally ask a bus boy, who brings it eventually. My wife's burger arrived with fries, everything looked great, but by the time salt and ketchup arrived everything was cold. This is not unusual here, but I can no longer excuse it as growing pains.
And they don't pay the liquor tax?!?! This is the only restaurant in Nashville charging the customers for it - even Kayne Prime, home of 50 cent charge per blue cheese olive in your drink, doesn't charge liquor tax. Really, between food prices and liquor tax, I would not suggest eating here.

The ugly:
Sound problems. It carooms off the back wall so you can't hear vocals at all if there's a band - of the 3 we've seen, this was a problem with all of them. It's all right for an acoustic act like Taj Mahal, but something needs to be done. Who opens a club in Nashville without consulting a sound engineer? Everyone in my party, each time, was disappointed in the sound quality.
Seating is, to put it bluntly, horrendous. At first glance, it's very pretty - until you realize that a) no matter where you sit, you're not facing the stage, and b) chairs are tiny, and tables are about a foot shy of the standard 2 or 4 seat table length. What this means is that no matter how much you pay, or what you reserve, you're going to be miserably uncomfortable. My wife is petite, our daughter is likewise, but even they complained that they couldn't eat without elbowing one another. 
The sideways-only seating means you don't get to enjoy the show the way you would with concert-style. I understand you can't do the concert-style and serve dinners, but I'd love to see this place change up so half the table is facing the stage. The other half could just turn their chairs around for the show. As it is, no one was happy with the seats.

All in all, I will continue to attend when I'm in town, because they're bringing in a lot of acts you wouldn't normally see in Nashville. But I'll dine elsewhere. And I'll try to get validated, even if I'm not a "vinofile" (because I resent paying $75 a year for what I would get), and I'll avoid ordering liquor.

First, the reviews here. Saying "Some of the best sushi I've had in Nashville" is already a tip-off. Nashville is not known for its sushi. Additionally, most of the Japanese restaurants in Nashville specialize in rolls, sometimes the weirder the better. Regular Japanese fare, like tsukemono (pickles), or good rice, go by the wayside.
My wife and I had a sudden hunger for Japanese food - sushi for me, stir fry and gyoza for her. After checking the reviews here and on other sites, and looking at on-line menus, we set out for Osake (or O'sake) with high hopes, already hungry for agedashi tofu, Japanese pickles, miso-yaki (cod) and several other dishes hard to find in Nashville. 
Let me say this first - they have finally posted a correct menu on their own website. Almost every other menu, including their Facebook site, is wrong. The Menuism site in particular has their old menu, with mouth-watering items like soft shell crab and Nabeyaki Udon. None of them were available.
Apparently, the original menu, which looked fantastic, needed to be "dumbed down" for Nashville and the Vanderbilt students who frequent this area. So no agedashi tofu. No Japanese pickles. No anything we'd gone for in the first place.
The waitress was very nice, but seemed stunned that any online menu was incorrect. (Of course, she also thought their delivery service delivered to the local hospital wards, which was completely incorrect as well.)
We were mightily disappointed, but starving, so we went ahead and ordered a few things. Here's the list:
-- Vegetable gyoza, one order, very average. Tasted like the ones you buy from Trader Joe's, only not as well cooked. Sauce that came with them was miniscule, we had to ask for more.
-- Shrimp shumai, one order, also average. Small amount of sauce but enough. However, no mustard, though they brought it on request.
-- House salad with ginger dressing (came with stir fry). The dressing resembled the old Ben Kay dressing , very creamy and tasting of mayonnaise, weirdly enough. No discernable ginger. Basic iceberg lettuce. 
-- Shrimp stir fry noodles (one order) were good enough that we'd order them again. A surprising amount of large shrimp, everything tasted very fresh. Unusual for a stir fry restaurant around here.
-- Salmon sushi (one order, two pieces, same as the below) - average at best. Pretty tasteless.
-- Tuna sushi - ditto.
-- Ikura sushi - slightly better than average. 
-- Steamed pork bun (one order) - good, would order again.
The chef was good, I'll give them that. But our meal for two - consisting of the above, lunch menu, was over $50!!!
Given that the place was completely empty at lunch hour, if I were them I'd go back to what the previous owner was doing. We were all set to make this our "go-to" Japanese restaurant, but I don't think we'll be back.

My wife and I went here because it had been recommended by so many of our local acquaintances. We went for Sunday brunch. She had the huevos rancheros, and I sprang for the $38 "no limit" buffet bar.
Let me say first that the biscuits are, ridiculously enough, a revelation. I have had many servings of Southern biscuits, and never really understood what the fuss was about. Now I get it. Light, flaky, just moist enough to whet without sticking to my palate. Astonishing. I could have made a meal of them.
The wait service was extremely attentive, and though I wish our waiter had spoken a bit more slowly, it's possible he was new and just anxious. Over-explaining in a rushed manner is sometimes as bad as under-explaining, but once I asked him to slow down a bit because I had trouble following him, he did immediately. He also kept a very close eye on all the tables, as did every other waiter in the room.
Our reservation was for the very start of brunch; no problem with parking or seating. The restaurant itself has a nice, open feel. Having a visible kitchen is always comforting to me, since I travel so much and am leery of food poisoning. The chefs, likewise, were extremely friendly. All questions were answered forthrightly.
The "huevos rancheros" did not look like any we'd ever seen. It was mostly beans and rice (both on the side), with the rest heaped over a tortilla shell. Pretty presentation, but I wouldn't recommend it. The side of bacon was small but absolutely delicious.
I did ask my waiter about the Live Band Louisiana Oysters, since I'd never heard of them. Once I'd convinced him I actually knew all the other oysters on the menu, he was frank and told me that they were popular, but he considered them the least worthy on the menu. Largely because of the oysters, which looked fine, I ordered the top of the line version of their buffet. I should have listened. They were absolutely awful - and this is from someone who's eaten raw oysters all over the world. Our entire party tasted them, and we were shocked that a restaurant of this caliber would serve oysters this bad. Perhaps it's still the oil spill - I hear there are inches of sludge remaining on the bottom of the ocean because of it - but these were dreadful. They were fresh, though - I watched them being shucked.
The charcuterie items were delicious, one and all. I'd particularly recommend the homemade coppa and the ham. The salads were fresh to a fault, and when I mentioned that my wife was allergic to eggs, they actually prepared two of the small wedge salads just for her. As noted, the service was excellent.
Another point in their favor - I picked up half a dozen of the boiled shrimp, but on peeling, found them all to be "mushy". I don't know why this happens, but it seems to happen quite often in restaurants. I've only had the problem cooking them at home once, and that was the fault of the shrimp (my bad for choosing them!). I mentioned it to the waiter, who brought over a manager, who looked at them and had them removed. Not just from my plate, but from the entire buffet.
That was impressive, because there'd been a fortune in shrimp sitting there.
The salmon was a bit disappointing, average. The salads were good but not remarkable. We found some of the food combinations strained, as though the chefs were working hard to make their menu "memorable". But the Brie with candied figs was excellent, as were all the other cheeses - easily the best "cheese plate" in Nashville. 
Another outstanding item was the coffee. We were disappointed that they didn't have espresso, but after one whiff, we forgot our worries and settled in to enjoy what is possibly the best cup of coffee I've had in America. 
Was the buffet worth $30? are the food items worth the tariff? I don't personally think so, but then again, I don't need to know the name of the farmer who grew my vegetables, or the location of the farm my meat came from. And if you want absolutely farm-to-table completely homemade items, I suppose it would be worth it. 
I'd recommend Urban Grub for a business lunch meeting over any of the other upscale spots I can think of here. It's quieter (we got seats by the window, which was smart), and though we found the piped in music annoying (how nice it would be, for once in this town, to have classical music at brunch!), that was a small price to pay.
Speaking of price, yes, it is pricey if you order a few different things - but choose carefully and you won't go wrong.
Would we eat there again? Yes, if we were in the neighborhood. I wouldn't call it "destination dining" but it's friendly enough, the food is mostly excellent, the service ditto, the seating comfortable. And honestly, I'd go back for the coffee! We're planning to try it for dinner at some point.
One minor note - be aware that the menus available on line are incorrect.

We were so terribly excited to try Little Octopus, being huge fans of Otaku. We wondered how they'd do, with what we'd heard was an upscale mostly-vegan menu. We found out. 
Our reservation was for start of business on a Saturday, and they opened on time. There were already a few people waiting, which we found encouraging.
The first impression was, sad to say, cheapness. The furnishings look hastily put together or purchased at downscale yard sales. The chairs are comfortable enough, but the high table stools need backs, especially if they want to encourage drinking and sitting in enough comfort to keep ordering. When I mentioned to my wife that the furniture looked like it was from Ikea, she said "No, Ikea looks nicer."
The ceilings are black, high, with everything showing. That was an interesting style when it first surfaced in the 70's New York loft scene, but not any more. I'm sorry to say this because I really wanted to love the decor. But it's cold, unfriendly, LA-modern-circa-1987.
Our waitress was annoying in that she kept forgetting everything, even though she'd written it down. When she first brought water (which was filtered and quite good by the way), I covered my glass and said "I'd like ice in it please", but as soon as my hand was removed, she poured the water anyway. About five minutes later, she remembered to bring the ice, in a teeny tiny glass.
Fortunately, the hostess filled in the blanks, and she was marvelous. The waitress did improve over the course of the meal, so perhaps it was just a bad day.
I would highly recommend the lemonade. It was fresh, tart, not too sweet, just delicious. The green gazpacho, which had been touted highly by a reviewer, was all right, but not fantastic. We did enjoy the fingerling potatoes with chimichurri sauce - not too much sauce, and the broccoli was a terrific addition. 
One previous reviewer noted that the dishes do not come out in the expected order, eg appetizers first, mains second. This is very Japanese, but also very annoying. When you're trying to eat a cold bowl of soup, and your hot main arrives almost immediately after you begin, it's annoying. The only solution we thought of would be to insist on ordering only appetizers, and when done, ordering mains. However, our waitress seemed to be in quite a rush to get the whole order in, so be forewarned.
I was excited to try the tofu, likewise touted in several reviews, but was very disappointed. I'm a big tofu fan, but American tofu is all about tastelessness to begin wtih, so the sauce or seasoning is really important. This tofu was, in a word, boring. Two slabs, with forgettable seasoning (actually, tasteless and burnt). I'd never have known it was sumac, which I've had before with tofu overseas and which can be delicious. It became more edible when I smeared it with the charred eggplant puree, but that was so salty it became uncomfortable, and I wound up not eating most of it.
My wife had something else for her main which was so forgettable that neither of us can remember what it was, even after looking at the on line menu. 
Another criticism - the music was LOUD. I don't mean loud, I mean LOUD. That would have been fine at night, with a bar crowd, but at 11 o'clock in the morning it was really annoying. To be fair, they turned it down when several tables complained, but it was also uneven. Maybe they made their own mix tape and forget to level the volume on it? I don't know, but it was annoying.
We were disappointed enough in the food that we didn't bother trying the desserts. In fact, we were glad to leave.
Again, we had very high hopes, but we wouldn't bother trying this again. They were off to a rocky start, from what I can garner from the reviews, and perhaps the owner(s) are just stretched too thin at this point. 
I am finding, on this trip, that Nashville's new restaurants in general are over-hyped, or perhaps mostly attended by people who are not good cooks themselves and haven't eaten in many great restaurants. The city's foodies still seem to be playing catch-up with major cities like LA and New York, or Chicago or Philadelphia. I'd give a lot to be able to visit a regular old-fashioned diner here, if everyone is being so "adventurous", or a really great Italian restaurant (please don't send me to Mama Mia's, they're uneven at best.) I'm thrilled at the preponderance of local farmer's markets, local dishes, organic foods - and curious to try Avo and Two-Ten Jack next trip - but in general, this is still not a great food town. Sadly.
I'm just hoping the "new" Otaku will be as good as the old!!!

My family LOVED the Green Hills Grille. We were among its first customers ever, even before the kids came along. We ate brunch there every Sunday we were in Nashville, for years. Spent anniversaries, Mother's Day, kid's birthdays, you name it. Grew to love the staff, Patty the cook and Andy the cook (steaks par excellence, really a talented great chef), the servers, the management. We went so much that one of the original owners, Phil, recognized us and came over and said "Hi" now and then.
It started going downhill, then suddenly there were three close relatives running the place, managing it, managing the kitchen. It got a little weird. But the food was still great - their "10% plus" stayed in effect (if your food wasn't to your liking, you got your meal picked up along with a gift cert plus 10%), the steaks were optimal, the spinach dip and chips way above anything else in town. The bar was pretty darned good too, but most of all, the food was consistent. Not a huge menu, but always the same. And always good.
So you can imagine how excited we were to hear they were re-opening. We went the third week, figuring they'd need time to settle. Got steak. Crappy meat. Got potatoes; no resemblance to the old Grille. 
"What does this menu remind you of?" I asked the wife. Ummmm. Mere Bulles?
Yeah. Mere Bulles. Or rather, kind of half Mere Bulles and half Green Hills Grille, with a dollop of "Why on earth is this even on a menu?"
I talked to some of the staff. "Where's Andy working, isn't he back here?" No, he's not in the kitchen. "Where's Patty, isn't she back here?" No, she's not here. "Why is my food cold/why did I have to wait 35 minutes for my salad/why doesn't my waiter write down my order instead of bringing all the wrong dishes/who's the kitchen manager or chef back there and why does everything taste like someone's experiment?"
Good questions.
Turns out the GHG "executive chef" is the brother of the owner/manager, and does double-duty as exec. chef at Mere Bulles. Hm.
If you want to eat at Mere Bulles, go there. It's right up the road in Brentwood. But we really wanted to eat at the Green Hills Grille.
Maybe someday they'll decide what they want to be, if they want to be the GHG or Mere Bulles. They're certainly doing enough business that it must not matter to them. But for those of us who remember fantastic ribs, great steaks, real spinach artichoke dip, and the best baked potatoes ever, this place is a real let down.

My children were visiting during school break, and all they kept talking about was Krispy Kreme. I bought them two dozen, which were gone in a day. Next day same thing. Third day was Saturday, and I was NOT travelling miles to go to Krispy Kreme. So I brought home two dozen assorted from Donut Den.
"WOW. Why haven't we ever had these before?!?! They're SOOOOO much better!"
That's my review. Just soooo much better!!!

Mmm. We went here because one of our friends is in search of the ideal pizza, worldwide. I wish we'd gone to Joey's, even though it would have been considerably further away. 
Avoid the prosciutto. Ours tasted like it had been sitting out for a while. Tough, chewy, and unlike any prosciutto we'd ever had. The waitress was attentive and pleasant, but everything she suggested was prefaced be "This is very popular" and "This is really popular". 
The spaghetti with white clam sauce and rabe was so salty, it was almost inedible. The margharita pizza "D.O.C." (very very special, we were told - has to be certified, special Italian sauce, etc) was average or less, especially if you've had great pizza in New York or even Italy. The calamari were average, on a bed of potato chips (and to be fair, the chips were pretty good). The calamari sauce was semi-warm and boring. 
The shrimp pasta was all right, completely forgettable. It would have been nice if our waiter had been even vaguely familiar with the wine list. The evening was capped by an order of cappuccino that was so badly made, it was actually cold - cold enough that it could have been in the refrigerator and pulled out for the occasion, with someone forgetting to warm it.
All in all a complete disappointment, and we won't try it again.

My spouse and I were very pleased to come back to Green Hills and see a new Greek restaurant. After checking the online reviews, we decided to have lunch there. Very disappointing. 
The restaurant's inside looks neat and clean, with two rows of booths. It was a little confusing at first, because in order to see the menu posted on the wall by the cash register, we had to stand next to the people ordering, which meant when they turned around toward the food bar, there we were, in the way. But that's a minor detail (though I wish there'd been menus available to grab and sit down with, since the posted menu was much more confusing than their on line menu or hand out.)
The first problem was speed. Although there were exactly two other customers in the restaurant, who'd finished ordering by the time we began, the cashier made us feel like we had to order as quickly as possible and get out of the way. Even though I said twice "We're still trying to decide", he kept asking what we wanted and rushing us along.
The second problem was language. English being my second language, I have empathy for anyone speaking with an accent here. Especially in the south, many ears aren't attuned to "hear" English spoken with an accent. However, mine are. I speak several languages, as does my wife, and we're used to dealing with Europeans from all over the place. So when neither of us can understand what people are saying, there's a problem that didn't originate with us.
In addition to the rush from the cashier, we could only catch about half what he said. Unfortunately, that continued as we passed through the food bar trying to tell the other two employees what we did and didn't want. And although the gentleman who seemed the "main" employee kept smiling, it was obvious his English was so limited that discussion was impossible. (For instance, "Please not so much sauce" or "Please more sauce" worked. "I don't want onions" did not, whereas "No onion, no onion" did.) 
Again, with only two other customers in the restaurant, we were still rushed through as quickly as possible.
Our next problem was something that happens, but is still quite a turn off - one of the customers before us brought his tabbouleh salad back because there was a large hair sticking out of it. The main server grabbed the plate with a big smile, took it in the back, came out smiling and saying "Plate. Plate." which I guess meant he thought the hair was a piece of the plate? He then proceeded to try and give the customer another tabbouleh salad (which was refused; the customer asked for a regular salad instead).
No apology. That's a big mistake, in my book. When someone finds a large hair in their food, I expect wait staff or management to apologize, pick up the cost of the meal or offer something free, and be very, very embarrassed. There was none of that.
Possibly the language difficulty, I don't know.
The fourth and last issue is the food. The gyro meat was very good, although there wasn't as much of it as we'd expected for the price. Salads were average at best. The tzatziki sauce was more than forgettable; it was, again, watery. Dull. No chunks of cucumber. No mint. Just bland. I even took a teaspoon of it and swished it around in my mouth, to see if it tasted like anything, but it did not.
The hummus was likewise eminently forgettable, and served without oil or lemon or even a few flakes of parsley. When I asked for lemon, I got an uncomprehending look.
The felafel were good, tasted fairly fresh, oval and sort of flat. Crispy on the outside and juicy on the inside. For some reason, they're served with feta cheese on top. The feta cheese was fairly tastelesss, unfortunate because I do love good feta!
I did get a small container of hot sauce when I asked. 
The baklava looked good, though we didn't taste it.. 
It was over $30 for the two of us: one salad with gyro sandwich (no rice or anything), one hummus appetizer, one small Greek salad, one felafel appetizer, and two drinks. That seemed high to me, given what we got. When I protested at the cash register, asking for an itemized bill, I was given a blank look.
Perhaps - just perhaps - we hit it on a bad day. If I had to eat here again I would order a felafel appetizer. Maybe even a gyro sandwich, with extra meat, and lots of onion to make up for the lack of flavor in the sauce. But between the rushing, the hair and lack of apology, and the blandness of the food, I don't believe we'll try this restaurant. again.

Here is what I try to do before reviewing a restaurant:
-- Eat there 3x, at different hours,with varying group sizes. 
-- Make sure one of those visits is off-hours. In this instance, arriving at 4:30 pm once, , as well as our previous experiences there.
I find that many times, when a restaurant stays open from lunch through dinner, there's a "slack-off" period that starts about an hour after lunch rush, and continues until an hour, maybe two , before dinner rush begins. 
For me, that period is the true test of how well a restaurant is run, and how well it's managed. Do they have an intermediate chef or cook who's in training, or just not as good as the regular person? is the staff sloppy, hanging on their phones or talking among themselves while customers sit and wait? Does the bathroom need attending, which will sometimes wait until just before the crush?
Perhaps it's too much to expect, but I assume a restaurant that serves terrific food at 8 pm will serve something just as terrific at 4 pm or 5 pm. I assume.
Started by Arnold Myint, whose mother Patty Myint has been a force for good, fresh Asian cooking in Nashville since 1975, PM began as a lovely neighborhood hangout with good sushi, interesting appetizers, and great drinks. 
Then, Arnold got famous. Top Chef. Food Network. Heady stuff. He opened two other restaurants in Nashville - Suzy Wong's House of Yum (sometimes excellent, especially for vegetarians. Sometimes not. Spotty.), and BLVD Bistro. In addition, he's "beverage consultant" for Rock Sugar Pan Asian Kitchen in Los Angeles, and a partner in Show Pony Wine. 
A busy fellow. Maybe too busy to stop into his signature restaurant and check on it during off-peak hours. Maybe too busy to ask an anonymous friend to stop by and make sure the food is still up to par. I don't know, but I hope he begins to pay more attention to PM, because it used to be great.
This wase one of our "go-to" places when visiting Nashville. Even though the music got louder and louder, and the food experiments became questionable, we kept trying. But after yesterday I doubt we'll try again.
"Laotian sausage". Interesting. Very very spicy. We realize that after decades of Nashvillians thinking adding white pepper made a dish too spicy, there's some catching up to do, but food shouldn't be so spicy that it can't be enjoyed. Still, the over-all taste was good.
The dirty Tito's martini, ordered "as cold as they can make it", was lukewarm. To be fair, it was lukewarm on our last two visits as well. Perhaps that's the new vogue. Oh, and watch out for the green olives - they're huge, and since they're so big, they raise the line of the liquid, so you actually think you're getting a full drink. You're not.
The "spicy scallop roll, easy on the mayo" was indeed easy on the mayo, but they compensated by putting about half a teaspoon of Sriracha on every piece. Again, there's spicy-wonderful, and spicy-for-the-sake-of-trendy-spicy, like this.
"Japanese hot dog" - we normally love the darned things. Described as "angus frank, tempura crisps, bacon, nori spicy sesame slaw, mustard, togarashi, scallions", it was actually a lukewarm  sausage (I'd almost swear it was your basic Polish sausage), with very little slaw (perhaps half a teaspoon), lukewarm soggy bacon, and a gigantic bun - not like the authentic Banh Minh buns served at Interasian Market in Nashville, not like the French baguettes, just a giant piece of tasteless bread re-formed into a hot dog bun. And the "dog" itself? Lukewarm. Just like the martini, only bigger.
Sweet potato fries were good, but soggy and lukewarm. Yes, really. It would have been great if they'd been crisped up somehow, instead of flopping over when we held them. But I will say, they were tasty.
The worst experience was the "Thai beef lettuce wraps". When I asked what kind of beef, the waiter shrugged and said "it's our beef." From that, I assumed it would be a portion of sirloin, since that's what they normally serve for beef. 
If this was sirloin, it was a very nervous cow. The dish was pretty to look at - large pieces of Romaine lettuce to the right, beef in the center, a bowl of rice to the left. The beef was lukewarm; in fact, I would not hesitate to use the word "congealing" to describe its sauce. 
The meat itself was nowhere near sirloin. I actually wondered, for a few minutes, if it was in fact beef. Despite the sauce that stuck to it like the worst of cheap Chinese restaurant food, over-dosed with corn starch, the dish was tasteless. Worse than tasteless. 
All in all, this was the worst meal we've had in a while. Unfortunately, our experiences at the same restaurant over the past six months have been about the same - though the Thai wrap with shrimp tempura seems to have held steady, and the beer is usually nice and cold. We won't be trying it again, sad to say. In fact, we'll probably go across the street to Patty Myint's International Market, where the food is consistent and not quite so "precious".

I've been eating breakfasts and lunches here since last fall, when a friend took me here for Sunday breakfast. I eat here twice a week or more, always bringing friends and colleagues. Because when it's good, it's terrific. I love that you can get a Cobb salad at 8 in the morning, or an omelette at noon. 
It's a great choice for breakfast between 7-9 am. Good choice for lunch at peak hours. What drives me absolutely up the wall is the inconsistency. Every single time I've been here at off peak hours, when apparently the cooks rotate, the food is miserably different from the peak hour food.
For instance. My sunnyside up eggs at peak hours are always perfect. Always. And at non-peak, not.
For instance. The new home fries are great, and at peak hours, they come perfectly browned, crisp on the outside. I would even say they're "thrilling" because it's so rare to get home fries perfectly cooked. But non-peak hours? Soggy. 
For instance. I've had the portabello mushroom tortilla at least fifteen times. Twelve of those times, it was among the best I've ever had - big juicy chunks of mushroom, fresher than fresh pico de gallo, and someone had the sense to cook the mushrooms and then drain them so the tortilla wasn't soggy. But the other two times? The guacamole was actually dark brown, and off. The pico de gallo was mushy. And the mushrooms gave off so much juice that the whole quesadilly was soppingly wet.

And then. The patty melt we ordered last week, which came without the Thousand Island dressing, which covered exactly half the bread, which was an embarrassingly small piece of meat that really shouldn't have been part of a patty melt in the first place.
One of my colleagues said yesterday "It's a real shame, this inconsistency, but what can we do?" And I responded - post in comments. Write to the GM. Send things back when they are not right. But frankly, when we are there for breakfast, we have somewhere to be right after, so we can't wait for them to re-do the food. Same with lunch. 
There was a GM, Chris, who seems to have left, and I've noticed a marked turndown since then. I really hope this gets turned around. My children, my wife, everyone we know loves going there - but they need to do something about the consistency.
One more note. The wait staff are exceptionally friendly and exceptionally on top of it. Apparently table stations are rotated, which means it doesn't bother them if you sit for a long time. 
One last note. The turkey and avocado skillet gives the impression it will be fresh turkey. In fact, it's poor quality pre-packaged smoked turkey. Nashville's grown too much for that.
Sorry, folks.

Pros: Extensive menu with interesting dishes (though the crawfish, which they didn't advertise and we only discovered was available a few days ago, quite by accident, has been discontinued.)
Clean restrooms. Casual sloppy ambience. Clean restrooms.
Cons: Horribly trained staff. The word "ultra-hipster" comes to mind; I'd trade the hip factor for competence. Each time we've been here, the person who greeted us looked like it was a real bother. Our first time, the waiter was an aspiring songwriter with a good attitude, but the kitchen kept messing up the order. This last time, we ordered  a "Tito's straight up as cold as they can make it" (which any bartender should have known was a martini) and a "Club soda". Granted, our waitress was young, but her training was non-existent. She put in the order as "Vodka mixed with club soda", which the bartender proceeded to make. (Did it not occur to ask whether that was correct? Perhaps we wanted an olive, or a twist of lemon?) Sent it back; bartender got annoyed and threw some cold vodka (maybe Tito's? maybe not?) in a regular water glass. Have they not heard of martinis?
Grease. The "fried squid with spicy mayo" was greasy enough that it required pressing between napkins to make it edible. I don't mind a little fat, but when it spurts out as I put a fork in, it's too much. 
Poorly worded menu. Fried squid's "spicy mayo" consisted of a dish of mayo and a dish of Sriracha, separately.
The banh minh bread was not very good; for those sandwiches I'd still recommend InterAsian Market; definitely the best baguette in town.
Last but very far from least, the pho isn't great. We've had the chicken, vegetarian, and beef. The chicken featured 5 small strips of chicken, not even 3" long and barely 1/4" thick. The vegetarian was so-so. I really wish the beef was organic, because I've known two people who died of Bovine spongiform encephalopathy  (Mad cow disease), and I'm extremely leery of eating any beef made with bones that aren't from an organic, grain-fed or pasture-fed source. You may think that's ridiculous, but the organic tastes much better as well. 
A pity, really.

I've been to Vui's seven or eight times now, and somehow, my tastebuds still aren't satisfied.
Pros: Very, very clean. From the prep area (right behind the ordering counter) to the bathrooms to the small dining porch, everything is spotless.
Most of the food is wonderful. From what I understand, the owner prepares the pork herself, and let me tell you, the banh minh sandwich couldn't be improved. 
Spring rolls are fresh, pretty basic, but very very tasty. Get them with the fish sauce instead of peanut sauce if you want a real treat.
The noodles with shrimp use real, plump, juicy shrimp - not those cheap tiny ones Miss Saigon has been using, and not the cheap dehydrated-then-fattened-with-who-knows-what-injected places like Kien Giang have been using. No, these are real shrimp, cooked just enough to be tasty.
The lotus salad is unusual, especially in Nashville, and delicious. (Though unlike most of the food, it isn't just as good the next day. Eat it all here.)
Decor is pleasant and unassuming. There are wonderful posters on the walls showing what ingredients go into each item as well.
Vegetarian options abound - we haven't found anything that couldn't substitute tofu or more vegetables for meat or poultry.
Cons: I hate to say it, but the pho is really substandard. I've eaten pho all over the United States, as well as several Asian countries, and this is not it. I was very very excited to try it, because my wife has problems with MSG, and so far as we've been able to discover, this is the only Vietnamese restaurant in Nashville that doesn't use it. But the pho just doesn't cut it. The boldness of Vietnamese flavors is missing. We've tried the steak pho (meat was okay, pretty tough, pieces quite thick), and the vegetarian pho (mushroom base, way way too mushroom-y for either of us). I wish they'd do a plain chicken pho, the kind you can buy for breakfast all over Viet Nam. 
Other con: The music. I'm sorry, but in a music town, playing below-average thrasher or metal music, or even heavy rock, at volumes that preclude table talk, is just not good. I was actually pretty surprised by the choice of music. To me, Vui's should be playing something classical, and playing it so quietly that I'd have to strain to make it out.
I've read a number of reviews that complained about the price. To me, paying $8.95 for an incredible sandwich with highest grade pork, no artificial anything, and super-fresh vegetables is just fine. My only quarrel with the banh minh is the bread, advertised as "baguette" but in reality a very soft long bun. Baguettes traditionally have crunchy crusts. This restaurant could take a lesson in that from our other favorite Vietnamese in town, Interasian Market, whose baguettes are as close to French bread as I've had in the States.
So, with the caveat that the pho could really use some help, I'd give this a high recommend.

They were improving. Honestly, they were! New owners, imported chefs. No MSG. Using potato starch instead of corn starch. Oh, they still didn't have spareribs, and the food was hit or miss, depending on which chef you got, but they were actually turning into a real Chinese restaurant.
We had high hopes of an actual Chinese menu, complete with jellyfish.
Alas and alack. All their energy - and their good staff, and their good chefs, and Joyce the hostess who actually listened and went to bat for things like "Please, make it really hot!" - are all concentrated on their dim sum restaurant. (I've only been there once, it was miserable, but in fairness I would try it again just in case.)
Our order tonight, and thoughts on same
Hot & Sour Soup: Oh for Pete's sake, this is a staple! We ordered a large, which turned out to be hot liquid poured into two cheap plastic containers. The soup was all right once I doctored it with a ton of chili oil. 
Moo Shu Chicken, no egg: Pancakes were actually under-cooked, tasted like raw dough. Moo Shu was pretty tasteless.
Brown rice: Was okay. Steamed, maybe. Flavorless.
Salted Crispy Whole Shellless Shrimp: 1. Was supposed to be spicy. Not. 2. Dreadfully overcooked. Dredged in something (flour? panko? who knows) and fried within an inch of their lives. If you tried to peel away the outside, the shrimp came with it. 3. With shells attached, as well as tails. 4. Tasteless.
Bok Choy with Black Mushroom: This used to be a house favorite, but it was so bad that we ended up throwing it out. How you can make something so tasteless is beyond me.

I really do wish Nashville had ONE "basic Western Chinese" restaurant. New York style. Garlic sauteed spinach. Spareribs. All the regular stuff.
By the way, they've gotten skimpy on the mustard, too. We got two containers, each about 1/4 full of hot mustard. Which wasn't hot.
As I said to my wife, "This is always a good reminder not to eat Chinese food in Nashville." Sad but true. Stick with Vietnamese and Thai.

I had hoped Whole Foods would get their act together, given the stunning amount of customer complaints and articles about the loss of their original "culture". But having been away four months and just returned, I see it's even worse.
Yes, the fruit and vegetables are beautiful. Yes, they're pretty much the only decent wide-selection fish market and organic meat market in town. That doesn't excuse what they've become.
Unfortunately, what used to be a great store has been turned inside out by the corporate powers-that-be. None of the original employees are there any longer - many have gone to Trader Joe's. The foods we like keep getting shoved out while 365 brand is shoved in. Items are moved around constantly, I guess on the theory that while you're searching for the Asian section or Nona Lim noodles (now with the pickles. Go figure), you'll see something else and impulse buy. 
As to the take-out food bars, I cannot for the life of me understand why everything in every WF is now exactly the same. Saving money is one thing; losing selection is another. For instance:
Get a plateful of cooked fish to take home - no tartar sauce. Request same. Get told we'd have to buy a jar.
Ask whether there's any salad spinach. Told no, none available, have to buy a bag.
Ask why there's no barbecue sauce or any kind of sauce for the barbecued meats and chicken. No one knows. But we could buy a bottle.
On top of that, the staff - mostly very young now, nothing wrong with that if they're well trained - spend much of their time huddled together, talking to each other. Customer service has a person available occasionally, but you have to wait. The fruit and vegetable people who used to know how to prepare things you'd never seen before are gone. 
I understand this is happening across the country. It's a real shame.

It's really too bad Johnny T. had such a bad experience, because it couldn't be further from ours - or most of the other reviewers.
My family get to Nashville often enough that we've eaten at just about every hot spot there is. Over the past 30 years, I've watched it grow into a truly multicultural city, and Plaza Mariachi (where Tres Gauchos is located) is a wonderful example of that growth. 
To say this restaurant is in a "food court" is a real misnomer. It's only a food court because there are multiple places to eat, and most share a central table area. By the way, the cleanest I've ever been to.
First, let me say that we've eaten at all the local steak places. We gave up on Kayne Prime a year ago when they took two of our favorite dishes off the menu, then insisted on charging me $1.50 for the three stuffed olives I had in my drink. (Really. Why not just raise the price of the drink?) We adore the steaks, and food in general, at The Palm restaurant, but downtown Nashville has gotten absurdly crowded, so we try to stay out of there when we visit. Ruth's Chris tends to be a little greasy for our taste, and behaves more and more like a chain. Fleming's is average at best, and Jimmy Kelly's was great in the 70's but now, outclassed.
We decided to go to Tres Gauchos spur of the minute on a Saturday. We got there just as they opened, and were disappointed to see that the pork ribs were only available after two. However, the chef agreed to cook them up anyway, and they were so good that we ended up getting several to-go orders for dinner.
Tres Gauchos serves chiaroscuro - meat cooked over an open wood-fired flame. You can watch the meat being cooked, a treat for kids.
We had the pork ribs, hangar steak, potatoes, and sirloin steak.
I thought the way you order was great - you take a form listing everything they serve, put an "X" over anything you want (including type of sauce or salsa), add your name and phone. Because everything is made to order, it takes 15-20 minutes, about what you'd expect in a regular restaurant. They text you when the order's ready.
I'm not going into particulars except to say that my hangar steak - cooked exactly as ordered, medium rare - was the best I've ever had. My wife said her ribs were among the best she's ever had. (She is from the South, they take these things seriously.) The people with us, eating skewers of chicken and of beef, said they were the best they'd ever had. And the sirloin steak was just amazing.
Because of the way the menu is arranged, it's easy for a group to order "something for everyone" and do a lot of tasting. The chimichurri verde sauce was excellent and freshly made, as was the red sauce. The corn was over-cooked, by my estimation, but that seems to be the American style of cooking corn; seasoning on it was delicious. Don't forget the potatoes, either!
* I noticed a couple of people becoming frustrated because the nice woman at the front (where you order) spoke limited English. If she can be patient, so can you! I found if I spoke slowly, all was well. At one point, we had some confusion when I wanted to know what the "meat of the day market price" was, and she said "cow". Several trips back and forth to the kitchen didn't bring more response than "Beef. From the side." But the chef was prepping, they weren't technically open yet, and later on he was kind enough to answer several questions for us.
Seriously high recommend. If we had stayed in town longer, we'd have gone back the next day!

Stopped in for a quick bite en route to our hotel - fantastic Cuban sandwich, large enough for two to split easily! My wife ordered the lechon asado/roast pork, which likewise was an enormous portion. It came with really good beans, rice, and loads of plantains. If I had it to do over again I'd order the pork with extra onion (the sauteed onion was terrific), and less rice on the plate (not that it was overwhelming, but the portions are huge.) 
Extremely friendly service and well priced. Very clean bathroom, too.
By the way, we got there just as they opened and were very glad we'd done so.
Highly recommend.

If you want sushi that smells like Clorox, this is the place for you. We went here because the two teenagers with us were starving, and it looked like the best out of a series of fast food restaurants surrounding it. The reviews were just all right, but again, very hungry teen boys who love sushi and Japanese food in general.
Normally, we can find something all right in a restaurant; the only thing I could recommend about Grill One Nine would be the cheerfulness of the server. Item by item:
The Saigon Won Ton soup was so greasy, you could actually see large globules of fat floating on the top. Even so, it was relatively tasteless.
Singapore lettuce wraps were served next to a "grouping" of iceberg lettuce leaves, which would have been great if they'd been cold, or fresh. Instead, they were lukewarm, and mostly limp. The chicken and nut in sauce next to them was lukewarm also, served with no spoon or fork (and pretty difficult to pick up with chopsticks). We did try picking it up with lettuce, but gave up pretty quickly because it made such a mess. Also, greasy.
House salads were an embarrassing blend of old iceberg and bad pseudo-ginger dressing.
Sunomono, which should have been assorted seafood and cucumber in a vinegar dressing, featured four "krabsticks", one limp shrimp, a few pieces of cucumber, a piece of what we were told was conch (but since it was tasteless, who knows...), and an inedible dressing.
Crunchy Fried Shrimp Served On a Bed of Crispy Rice Noodle could easily have come out of a box past its sale date, then microwaved. More "fried" than shrimp or crunch.
The biggest horror, however, was reserved for the "Sashimi-Tini". I made sure to ask what the fish would be, and was told tuna, salmon, and white fish. So they were, at least, at first appearance. When I bent over with chopsticks in hand, the main thing I could smell was disinfectant. At first, I thought perhaps the dish itself hadn't been rinsed properly, but it was actually the fish. Let me be clear. There was no "fishy" smell. It stunk of disinfectant. Clorox-like. Perhaps ammonia. The worst was the white fish (which was also not terribly white, and not very cold), followed by the tuna (two hacked pieces that could have been cut with a bread knife). I didn't try the salmon.
My biggest gripe, after a completely unsatisfactory meal that cost us more than $50 before tip, was that we obviously left most of the food on the table. Even the teenaged boys left theirs. And yet, the waitress was completely unaffected by the site of the untouched sashimi, or that we'd left at least half the food without touching it. 
This was, quite truthfully, one of the worst meals any of us had ever experienced. Maybe they changed owners or chefs recently, maybe we hit it on a bad day, maybe there's a reason the 2-4-1 and happy hours are advertised on the side of the building. We ended up stopping an hour later and hitting a generic pizza place to feed the boys.

I don't know how First Watch manage to be so consistent, state to state, city to city, but they are. This newest addition to Nashville's burgeoning breakfast scene (who knew you could eat something that wasn't drenched in gravy and grease for breakfast?) is a very welcome neighborhood hang. We've been to the other First Watch in this area, which is somewhat quieter (lower ceilings, better noise control), but with this right around the corner it's rapidly become our family's restaurant of choice for breakfast, brunch, and lunch.
Pros: Food as well as service are remarkably consistent. No matter how busy they are, waitrons act happy to see you. If something is wrong, it's fixed immediately, and if it takes too long (as happened with our well-done bacon order recently), they take it off the charges. The menu here is a bit smaller than other First Watches we've been to, but they'll make anything on the other menus if you request it. The managers are available for compliments as well as complaints. You can call ahead and warn them you'll be coming with a party of 4+, and they actually pay attention. In particular, we like the varied wait staff - varied ages, varied colors, varied "types". It's obvious people are hired for competence, skill sets, and enthusiasm. Their waffles are truly terrific, the salads big enough for two, and their Aztec cold brew is excellent.
The cons: Noisy when full. I mean, noisy. 75-80 on a decibel meter, the equivalent of trying to have a conversation in the middle of a crowded street with cars on either side. The rear seating has a little bit of noise barriers on the low ceiling, but I suspect that's more because they had to, cosmetically. Lots of glass and straight angles. This could be an easy fix by installing a few decent sound barriers a la recording studios, and give the restaurant (and high, ping-y ceiling) a bit more warmth. As it is, very difficult to hold a conversation when the restaurant is even half full.
Also, allergy awareness is not as high as at other FW's we've visited. My wife mentioned she was allergic to eggs and was assured the sandwich only had Dijonnaise, which contains mayo, which contains eggs. At several other FW's, a whole separate ticket is written for anyone with an allergy, and there's a big red line to warn the wait staff.
Last, the cold brew coffee (not the "iced coffee", which comes with milk and sweetener already in) is delicious - among the best we've had (though we wish it was a bit stronger). However, at close to $5 a glass, with not even one free re-fill, it's a bit over the top. Even Starbucks is cheaper for the same size.
I've looked at the other reviews, and I suspect the restaurant initially had "growing pains". We haven't experienced a very long wait for our food, and we've been at least a dozen times at various times of day. 
In general, a real pleasure to visit, and very glad they opened here!

Six of us (5 adults and one child) went to this CPK on a Sunday evening, early (5'ish). We got there plenty early to make sure it wasn't crowded (though I now understand why it wasn't). There were only five tables besides ours scattered throughout, all parties of 2-4 people. The only table with more people was just leaving. There was one person at the bar. That's it. 
First, our waiter couldn't be bothered to write a lot of things down (standards like "Could I get a glass of ice water please?" and "Could we get red pepper flakes for the pizza?"). He should have, because we didn't order a single thing that wasn't forgotten at least once.
When he finally bothered coming over, we ordered drinks - they arrived a full 10 minutes later (how hard is it to get ice water and seltzer?). We put in our food order pretty quickly. A full forty minutes later, we were still waiting for our appetizers - an order of cold asparagus, some flatbread, some pot stickers. The 5 year old was starving; we finally got a plate of bread, but nothing else. I got the waiter's attention and complained; he told us he couldn't say anything to the cook or the manager would get mad.
What? Why is this our problem? Why not just go to the manager?
Appetizers arrived at the 45 minute mark. No dressing for the asparagus. Cold flatbread. (He said "Gee, it was hot when I brought it out.") Cold pot stickers. I'm serious. And forget the drink refills we'd asked for 15 minutes earlier - he certainly did. 
I complained again and asked for the manager. "He's making the pizza." Seriously? on a Sunday night? "Well, we give priority to take out orders." Sorry, that's backward.
The restaurant still only had 8-9 tables filled with small parties (mostly two's) when our food arrived, 60 minutes after we'd placed the order. We ate it all because we were so hungry, even though the pizza with serrano peppers actually had jalapenos (ouch!) and it took another 10 minutes to get some Parmesan and red pappers, by which time the pasta was getting cold. 
Four of our party had desserts, which I'm told were very good. But after two fairly serious complaints, and an hour's wait for food (not counting the time it had taken our waiter to saunter his way over to us, the missed drinks, the cold appetizers), the restaurant charged 100% of what we'd ordered. 
We've been to this CPK on numerous occasions in the past years, and although it seemed to be sliding downward, it was never this bad before. What should have been a pleasant family evening really turned into a disastrously bad one, for no reason other than bad management and a waiter who didn't have the sense to take off a few items for good will. Extremely disappointing, and put us off the entire chain.

Maybe we should just have ordered pizza. As it was, stuck in a nearby hotel on a rainy evening, I took the front desk's advice and ordered from here. Seemed simple enough - a chicken hoagie with oil and vinegar, a salad, blue cheese dressing on the side, and that was it. 
Could they possibly have made the sandwich any blander? used any less oil and vinegar? sent decent blue cheese dressing instead of two small containers, one yellowed with age and one just tasting awful?
The bread was okay. The slices of chicken were edible. The salad lettuce was bitter, the two meager black olives straight from the can and not fresh enough to even have any taste. There was no salt or pepper, though they did include two knives and one fork. And lots of napkins.
That was about it. I wish I'd stuck with the hotel pantry's frozen food section...

I'm giving this a two only because judging by the other reviews, we hit the restaurant on a bad night and had a bad waitress. Also, the bread was good.  Otherwise, it would be a one. 
We went with friends and requested courtyard seating for the six of us, which we were given. Proof of vaccination required, which we appreciated. After being seated, our waitress - Ember - came and my husband gave her his gold American Express card with instructions to charge the entire meal to him. I don't know if that affected her or not, frankly, but she up-sold us so hard, and so fast, that my head was spinning. 
First, almost insisting we order cocktails and mocktails - one for each person. Heaven forbid anyone truly just wanted water. As we perused the menu we were pushed to order their combination meat platter. The waitress kept insisting she'd never been wrong yet, she could just tell what we wanted. She didn't bother listening to anything anyone said until my husband put his foot down and said "One of us doesn't eat meat!!! What is today's fish?" 
The bread came and it was excellent, but along with it came a push, again, to order the meat combination platter. I'd really been excited to order the rib-eye, my husband desperately wanted his own bone-in rib-eye,  my nephew wanted lamb chops - she completely ignored us and kept shoving the combo , insisting she would "know" what we wanted.
We had a vegetarian at the table as well, so we asked for side vegetables. Did we get to choose them? No. The order was put in without anyone ever agreeing to it. The waitress talked so fast, and was so intent on us having what she chose, that she just ran over us. 
The fish came, red snapper we were told, but you couldn't tell. It was so salty that when I was offered a taste, I almost had to spit it out. Inedible. The oblivious waitress never noticed that the fish was mostly untouched when the table was cleared. The combo platter came, too, and her proudest moment was showing us the marrow bones.
Again, we'd REALLY been looking forward to this - but sorry, the rib-eye was not good. Not at all. The shortribs, which she'd lauded as fall-off-the-bone, were stringy. Admittedly, the marrow bones were delicious, the presentation was great, but she never shut up long enough for us to get a word in edgewise. Lamb chops, such as they were, overdone to the point of tasting vaguely like liver. Not that she'd asked how we wanted anything other than the steak.
As to our poor vegetarian, the waitress had chosen our sides already - asparagus (5 pieces, each smaller than the last), pureed potato of some sort (not enough for three, let alone six), and French fries (not what we would have ordered in that restaurant.)
The drinks were good, though very sweet. We managed to order only one dessert, though she insisted on bringing every single one of us a plate and fork despite the vegetarian saying he wouldn't touch the dessert.
We were with local family and felt obliged to say nothing, since they'd been so excited to take us here. But we will never, ever go back. This was one of the worst dining experiences we've ever had. And at $175 a person including tip, very much not worth the price. And today, all of us agreed that we had never, ever, had such a pushy, overbearing wait person in our lives.

Hit this spot for our lead off night for Indy 500 weekend. After reading the yelpers suggestions, I made rezez for our party of 15.  Maybe its cuz I live in SoCal and have had many less than satisfactory experiences booking for large partys, I was expecting the worse, especially on the Friday night of race weekend. 

Well well well my little pretties, these mid-westerners really know customer service and how it is supposed to work. Tables all set up where promised (upstairs, overlooking the bandstand), reserved signs everywhere, Niki (I believe), waiting nearby to get us drinking ASAP, and very cheerful to boot. We were a disorganized lot as well; folks flying in at various times, some of us wanting to hit the sack early etc.  Sooo just to make sure we were an extra pain....lets ask for a few separate checks. OMG!!  This would cause most SoCal service peeps to go screaming to their managers to have these horrible customers set straight!  You know what Niki did? She smiled and said NO PROBLEM. What!?!  She was  extremely attentive with some help from her support crew and kept the drinks and food coming. 

The food was above average bar food, good for soaking up the booze, but to be fair we weren't really concerned about eating as much as catching up and drinking.....a lot.

In summary; the band was great, the crowd of varying ages was a typically friendly, mellow mid-western kinda group, awesome service, reasonably priced, just a great place to party. Not to be missed when in Indy.

Had a free night to dine with my Nephew while the rest of our Indy 500 crew of 15 went to the Snake Pit Black Tie Ball.  Bah Humbug!!  Like I'm gonna pack formal wear for an Indy 500 weekend!  So I searched yelp for something high end so we would have an experience to brag about as well. 14 happened to be 1/2 block from our Hampton Hotel, sweeeet!  And how sweet it was.

Since it was just us two guys we opted for the bar instead of the formalish dining room.  Good move!  I wish I could remember our bartender/servers name, but most everyone at the bar knew it, very friendly/local vibe for an upscale place. He was well informed re; the menu and put us out of towners at ease. I started with the spinach salad topped with a medium poached egg, nice addition. I also enjoyed the Indiana free range pork chop, a tad overcooked for my preference, but still very good. It was accompanied by the most incredible feta infused mashed potatoes. I am very partial to feta cheese so I was in Indiana Heaven! Nephew selected the lamb shank which was cooked to perfection, and came with polenta. Had a nice Hayman and Hill Pinot Noir that went well with both entres. 

Prices are what you would expect for the food and  ambiance, but not outrageous. The Ball earned the better bragging rights as the Ohio Players were the house band for the night, but no regrets on our part damn it!

On our way to San Luis Obispo it was time to take a restroom break, and I pulled off on a random exit. My nose for wine directed us to this nice looking tasting room. It was barely 11:00 on a Saturday morning and they were already doing some brisk business. Damn winos.

We were greeted by the friendly staff and decided to split a tasting. Those that know me are shocked I'm sure, but we still had a ways to drive. I do have my prudent moments. $10 for 6 tastes, and none were particularly memorable except for their Chardonnay. One of the best in memory. Big, bold, oakey, and buttery. Too big for most peoples taste but I love my Chardonnays like they were in the 80's. The other tastes were Pinot and some Italian style blends. Meh. 5 stars for the Chard however, and at $22 a bottle I should have grabbed a few more. I did confirm that High Times in Costa Mesa currently stocks it. On my way!  

If in the area or needing to take a road wizz, be sure to visit. The lady helping us said there are over 20 tasting rooms in this immediate area. Next time we may just book a hotel nearby and call it a weekend.

The vibe here is quintessential New Orleans. Loud, bustling, a sensory overload with the bar and oyster shuckers on one side, and the open kitchen just a few yards away on the other. Great friendly service but all business. Most restos in NOLA know how to turn tables like no other city, but they usually do so with a smile and some humor. And of course with their awesome Louisiana accent. Love it! 

The charbroiled oysters were off the chart buttery-garlicky delish.The Chicken/Andouille Gumbo sorry to say, not so much. Way too salty, although some at the table said the seafood gumbo was fine. The fresh oysters were just OK, not the best I have ever had. Others at the table loved the fried fish combo, and the shrimp that I stole from one was very tasty, and not too greasy. The hush puppies were also little fried wonders of great flavors. 

Hot tip: we arrived to zero line 30 minutes before the 11:00 opening and repaired across the street to Jesters for breakfast beers. When we wandered back at 10:50 there were only 4 ppl in front of us. This was on a Friday morning, so this tip is most likely invalid on a Saturday or Sunday. I have been to Acme many times and have never had a long wait, so it's all about planning and timing. We had a party of 6, so arriving early was a must. If just 2 ppl you can usually gain access to the bar fairly quickly, which is where you can watch the talented shuckers.

A never to be missed institution for me when in this wonderful city.

This is another one of those restaurants that already has so many reviews (almost 700 at this writing) that you consider not bothering to write another. Well eff that! Since this is one of the finest and most storied restaurants not only in New Orleans, but also of the entire USA I am adding one more. Plus I want the bragging rights that comes with dining in a special place such as Commander's Palace. 

This was my 3rd time visiting and the service is so good it teeters on being over the top. Almost. But the staff here are so professional and caring that it never reaches that point. Our waiter Roch was extremely knowledgeable about the menu and was hilarious as well. One of the most enjoyable dining experiences I have ever had. Also enhanced by the roving trio, which were also fun loving guys. My nephew jokingly requested King of The Road, and they insisted on giving it their best even though they didn't know all of the words. Some of us...ahem...even helped them along. Does that help convince you that this is not a stuffy place? Hopefully, because that is my point. These people are all about their guests having the time of their life. And we definitely did. 

And the food? Also incredible to match the service. My brunch entrée was the "Pecan Crusted Gulf Fish", which was drum fish on this day. Came topped with Prosecco poached Louisiana crabmeat, with pecans floating in the sauce that surrounded the fish. Excellent! Ordered the "Creole gumbo" as a starter, but one of my table mates had the turtle soup, and it definitely outshone my very good gumbo. Very rich and flavorful, probably one of the best soups I have ever had the pleasure of partaking. For desert I pre-ordered the bread pudding soufflé, and it was divine with the Roch recommended Quady "Essencia" Orange Muscat from California. Speaking of which, the wine prices are very reasonable. $8.50 for their branded chardonnay, that was more than drinkable. They even make a show of their "Classic Bloody Mary" by spiking it tableside with "ice block" vodka, and is mixed with their "award-winning housemade Bloody Mary mix."  Sounds like a $15 bloody Mary huh? Nope, a lousy $6.75.

So there you have it, one more superlative review of the legendary Commander's Palace. As I often say about New Orleans in general, I can't wait to return.

Fried Chicken!?! You're Kidding!?! That is what one of our party exclaimed when 2 of us that had been here previously mentioned that's what we were ordering. My buddy backed me up with "it's the reason they are in business." That might be a slight exaggeration, but the point was well made. Our doubter changed his mind later in the meal when I allowed him a generous taste. When his eyes widened upon his first bite I knew Praline Connection just won over a new convert.

Yep, the fried chicken is my favorite after 5 or 6 visits over the years. The catfish is always excellent as well as the greens, mac and cheese, and the red beans and rice. I remember the cornbread to be better than it was on this last visit, but maybe just an off night as it was a tad dry. The surprise hit was the fried alligator sausage I sampled. Juicy, a little spicy, very tasty, and I am not a huge fan of sausage. 

The service in most NOLA restaurants is super fast at the busy touristy French Quarter spots, and very professional at the higher end places. Here its kind of in between. They are very professional, but as is typical of the South outside of New Orleans its what I call Southern Slow Service. No one seems to see the need to rush, until the food is ready to come out of the kitchen, then all hell breaks loose. I guess the chef is prodding them to get it while its hot. But everything else from getting your beverages and set ups etc will get there when it gets there. Here it was almost comical how long it took to get a bottle of wine out from the back, and then another loooong process to uncork. In defense of our waiter we did have a party of 7, and he was pretty much on his own in addition to having several other tables. All of the staff just work on their own tables with out any thought of team work. I even warned our party beforehand to have patience as we were going to be there awhile. So sit a spell, relax, and enjoy the experience. It'll get here when it gets here y'all. 

But the food here is so awesome, and I can't think of any place else in NOLA or anywhere else that does good ol' Southern Soul Food like Praline Connection. So I will return each and every time I am back in my favorite foodie city. 

Laissez les bons temps rouler!!

Of course with a name like WINO, this was on my must hit list for our recent NOLA trip. It has the same type of enomatic self serve system like our beloved OC Wine Mart here in Orange County Ca. This place has at least three times as many choices though. Unfortunately we just came from a fine dining experience with a lot of wine, so I couldn't take full advantage. But we did what we could. Unlike OC Wine Mart you don't need to pre-load your smart card. When you are through tasting the attendant plugs the card into his POS system and walla, pay the man. You can also set your limit ahead of time to avoid any surprises at checkout. There are tastes from $1 on up, with some great wines, and not so great. Definitely a good variety of offerings. 

The space itself is split into two small separate seating areas, both very chill and comfortable. The one staff member was a little standoffish at first, but warmed up after we engaged him a bit. I jokingly called him on it and he sheepishly agreed, and said it was because he was from Boston. He humorously stated that he is comparatively more cheery and that his fellow Bostonians used to ask him where he was from. Funny! 

A great after dinner stop with a friendly mostly young and female clientele, at least on the recent Saturday night of our visit.

If you are a wino like moi, definitely worth a stop. Cool area of NOLA btw.

We were so caught up doing some of the best restaurants in New Orleans that on get-away-day we realized we hadn't had a proper old school po'boy. We saw Serio's a couple days previous as it is next to where one catches the bus for the St Charles Street Cars. One of our crew mentioned he had been years ago, and it was one of his favorite po'boy shops. After several days of NOLA debauchery I am surprised we even remembered that conversation. See, we must of not overindulged too much, huh?

Definitely a well worn old space, but in a good clean way. We we greeted very enthusiastically at the "order up" counter. Liking this place already. The friendly lady recommended the fried oyster/shrimp po'boy, and I of course chose a local Abita beer to wash it down with. After you place your order you take the few steps to the other side of the counter to pay. There we were met by Mike the very hospitable 3rd generation owner. 

Yep, great po'boy indeed. Hot, fresh, and I dowsed it liberally with locally made Crystal Hot Sauce. As the label states: "Louisiana's Pure." Perfect get-away NOLA lunch. 

So step a few blocks away from The Quarter and enjoy lunch in relative quiet with mostly locals.
